docs.title: Q: What is Salesforce's security model and how does it work?
docs.text:
A: Salesforce's security model is a layered approach that controls access to data at multiple levels, from the organization down to individual fields and records.

Security Layers:

  • Organization Level: Login access, password policies, network restrictions
  • Object Level: Determines which objects users can access via profiles and permission sets
  • Field Level: Controls visibility and editability of specific fields
  • Record Level: Determines which specific records users can view and edit through OWD, role hierarchy, and sharing rules

Key Characteristics:

  • Uses a "least privilege" approach - deny access by default, grant explicitly
  • Multiple layers work together - most restrictive setting wins
  • Declarative configuration requires no code
  • Can be extended with Apex sharing for custom logic

Example Security Flow:

// Checking object and field access before DML
if (Schema.sObjectType.Account.isAccessible() && 
    Schema.sObjectType.Account.fields.AnnualRevenue.isAccessible()) {
    List<Account> accounts = [
        SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue 
        FROM Account 
        WHERE Industry = 'Technology'
        LIMIT 100
    ];
}

Security Model Hierarchy:

  1. Can user log in? (IP restrictions, login hours)
  2. Can user see this object? (Profile/Permission Set)
  3. Can user see this field? (Field-Level Security)
  4. Can user access this record? (OWD + Sharing Rules + Role Hierarchy)
  5. Can user perform this action? (CRUD permissions)

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ All editions support basic security model
  • ✅ Professional Edition and above support role hierarchy
  • ✅ Enterprise Edition and above support advanced sharing rules

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Start with restrictive OWD settings and open up as needed
  • ✅ Use permission sets for additive permissions
  • ✅ Regularly audit user access using Security Health Check
  • ✅ Implement field-level security for sensitive data
  • ✅ Test security with different user profiles

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is Organization-Wide Default (OWD) and how does it affect data access?
docs.text:
A: Organization-Wide Default (OWD) is the baseline level of access that users have to records they don't own. It establishes the most restrictive settings for an object, which can then be opened up through role hierarchy, sharing rules, and manual sharing.

OWD Sharing Settings:

  • Private: Only record owner and users above them in role hierarchy can access
  • Public Read Only: All users can view records but only owners can edit
  • Public Read/Write: All users can view and edit all records
  • Controlled by Parent: For detail records in master-detail relationships
  • Public Read/Write/Transfer: Available for Cases and Leads only
  • Public Full Access: Available for Campaigns only

Key Considerations:

  • OWD can only be used to restrict access, never to grant additional access
  • Changes to OWD settings can take time to recalculate sharing
  • More restrictive OWD settings require more sharing rules
  • Cannot set OWD to Private for master objects in master-detail relationships

Example Use Cases:

  • Sales Organization: Set Opportunities to Private so reps only see their own deals
  • Support Team: Set Cases to Public Read Only so all agents can view but only case owners can update
  • Marketing Department: Set Campaigns to Public Read/Write so all marketers can collaborate

Configuration Steps:

Navigate to: Setup → Security → Sharing Settings

Governor Limits:

⚠️ OWD recalculation can take hours for large data volumes

⚠️ Defer sharing calculation option available for data loads

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Available in all editions
  • ✅ Private OWD requires Professional Edition or above for role hierarchy

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Set OWD as restrictive as business requirements allow
  • ✅ Use "View All" and "Modify All" permissions sparingly
  • ✅ Test OWD changes in sandbox before production
  • ✅ Document business justification for OWD settings
  • ✅ Review OWD settings quarterly as business needs evolve

Related Salesforce Features:

  • Role Hierarchy (opens access up)
  • Sharing Rules (opens access to groups)
  • Manual Sharing (opens access to individuals)
  • Territory Management (alternative to role hierarchy)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is the difference between a Profile and a Permission Set?
docs.text:
A: Profiles and Permission Sets both control user access in Salesforce, but they serve different purposes. Profiles define the baseline permissions every user must have, while Permission Sets extend those permissions for specific users without changing their profile.

Key Differences:

  • Profile: Required for every user (one per user), defines minimum access level
  • Permission Set: Optional, can assign multiple per user, grants additional permissions only
  • Profile: Can both grant and restrict permissions
  • Permission Set: Can only grant additional permissions, never restrict

When to Use Each:

  • Use Profiles for: Common baseline permissions shared by a group of users
  • Use Permission Sets for: Special access needs that only some users require
  • Use Permission Sets for: Project-based or temporary access requirements
  • Use Permission Sets for: Reducing profile proliferation

Example Scenario:

// You have 50 sales reps who need:
// - Profile: "Sales User" (base access to Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities)
// 
// 5 senior reps also need access to:
// - Permission Set: "Discount Approver" (ability to approve discounts over 20%)
// 
// 3 reps temporarily helping with marketing need:
// - Permission Set: "Campaign Manager" (access to Campaign objects)

Profile Components:

  • Object permissions (CRUD)
  • Field-level security
  • Tab settings
  • Record type assignments
  • Page layout assignments
  • Login hours and IP restrictions
  • Password policies (for some profiles)

Permission Set Components:

  • Object permissions (CRUD - additive only)
  • Field-level security (additive only)
  • Tab settings
  • App permissions
  • Apex class access
  • Visualforce page access
  • Custom permissions

Migration Example:

OLD APPROACH (Profile Proliferation):
- Sales User Profile
- Sales User with Marketing Access Profile
- Sales User with Discount Approval Profile
- Sales User with Marketing and Discount Profile
(4 profiles to maintain!)

NEW APPROACH (Profile + Permission Sets):
- Sales User Profile (1 profile)
- Marketing Access Permission Set
- Discount Approval Permission Set
(1 profile + 2 permission sets - easier to maintain!)

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Profiles available in all editions
  • ✅ Permission Sets available in all editions (introduced in Spring '12)

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 1,000 permission sets per org (can be increased)

⚠️ Maximum 1,500 permission set assignments per user

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Minimize number of profiles (aim for 10-15 maximum)
  • ✅ Use permission sets for additive permissions
  • ✅ Name permission sets clearly based on function (e.g., "API_Integration_User")
  • ✅ Use permission set groups to bundle related permission sets
  • ✅ Document the purpose of each permission set
  • ✅ Regularly audit permission set assignments
  • ✅ Clone existing permission sets to speed up creation

See Also:

  • Permission Set Groups (bundle multiple permission sets)
  • Muting Permission Sets (temporarily remove permissions)
  • Session-Based Permission Sets (temporary access)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How do I configure Field-Level Security (FLS) in Salesforce?
docs.text:
A: Field-Level Security (FLS) controls whether users can see and edit specific fields on an object. It works in conjunction with object-level permissions to provide granular data access control.

FLS Permission Levels:

  • Visible: User can see the field (read access)
  • Read-Only: User can see but not edit the field
  • Hidden: User cannot see or edit the field (most restrictive)
  • Editable: User can both see and edit the field (requires Visible + Edit)

Configuration Methods:

Method 1: From Profile/Permission Set

  • Setup → Users → Profiles (or Permission Sets)
  • Select profile/permission set
  • Find "Field-Level Security" section
  • Click field name → Set permissions

Method 2: From Field Settings

  • Setup → Object Manager → [Object] → Fields & Relationships
  • Click field name → "Set Field-Level Security" button
  • Configure for multiple profiles at once

Code Example - Checking FLS:

// Check FLS before querying
if (Schema.sObjectType.Account.fields.AnnualRevenue.isAccessible()) {
    List<Account> accounts = [SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue FROM Account];
}

// Check FLS before DML
Account acc = new Account(Name = 'Test Corp');
if (Schema.sObjectType.Account.fields.Industry.isCreateable()) {
    acc.Industry = 'Technology';
}
if (Schema.sObjectType.Account.isCreateable()) {
    insert acc;
}

// Checking multiple fields
Map<String, Schema.SObjectField> fieldMap = Schema.SObjectType.Account.fields.getMap();
if (fieldMap.get('AnnualRevenue').getDescribe().isAccessible() &&
    fieldMap.get('Industry').getDescribe().isAccessible()) {
    // Proceed with operation
}

Security Class Implementation:

public class SecurityUtils {

    // Generic FLS checker
    public static Boolean checkFieldAccessible(String objectName, String fieldName) {
        Schema.SObjectType objectType = Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(objectName);
        if (objectType == null) return false;

        Schema.DescribeSObjectResult describeResult = objectType.getDescribe();
        Map<String, Schema.SObjectField> fields = describeResult.fields.getMap();

        if (fields.containsKey(fieldName)) {
            return fields.get(fieldName).getDescribe().isAccessible();
        }
        return false;
    }

    // Check multiple fields at once
    public static Map<String, Boolean> checkFieldsAccessible(
        String objectName, 
        List<String> fieldNames
    ) {
        Map<String, Boolean> results = new Map<String, Boolean>();
        Schema.SObjectType objectType = Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(objectName);

        if (objectType != null) {
            Map<String, Schema.SObjectField> fields = 
                objectType.getDescribe().fields.getMap();

            for (String fieldName : fieldNames) {
                if (fields.containsKey(fieldName)) {
                    results.put(
                        fieldName, 
                        fields.get(fieldName).getDescribe().isAccessible()
                    );
                } else {
                    results.put(fieldName, false);
                }
            }
        }
        return results;
    }
}

Common Use Cases:

  • Sensitive Financial Data: Hide salary or revenue fields from non-management users
  • Personal Information: Restrict access to SSN, birthday, or personal contact info
  • Legal Compliance: Implement GDPR or HIPAA data restrictions
  • Competitive Information: Hide strategic data from certain user groups

FLS Interaction with Other Security:

Security Layer Priority (Most to Least Restrictive):
1. Field-Level Security (can hide fields completely)
2. Page Layout (controls visibility on UI, not data access)
3. Record Type (determines which page layout to use)
4. Profile/Permission Set (controls FLS settings)

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Available in all editions
  • ✅ Can be set via profiles in all editions
  • ✅ Can be set via permission sets in all editions

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 500 custom fields per object (FLS applies to each)

⚠️ FLS checks do not count against governor limits

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Always enforce FLS in Apex code using WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED or describe checks
  • ✅ Hide sensitive fields by default, grant access explicitly
  • ✅ Use permission sets to grant field access rather than modifying profiles
  • ✅ Test with different user profiles to verify FLS settings
  • ✅ Document business justification for field access
  • ✅ Use Security Health Check to identify FLS issues
  • ✅ Consider using Platform Shield Encryption for extremely sensitive data

Common Mistakes:

  • ❌ Not checking FLS in Apex code (security vulnerability)
  • ❌ Relying only on page layouts to hide fields (data still accessible via API)
  • ❌ Granting "View All Data" permission without understanding implications
  • ❌ Not testing field-level security with actual user accounts

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How do Role Hierarchies work and when should I use them?
docs.text:
A: Role Hierarchy in Salesforce is a tree structure that defines levels of data access. Users at higher levels in the hierarchy can access records owned by or shared with users below them, implementing a "ladder of access" model.

Core Concepts:

  • Upward Access: Users higher in hierarchy can access records of users below them
  • No Lateral Access: Users at same level cannot see each other's records (unless sharing rules permit)
  • No Downward Access: Users cannot see records of users above them
  • Applies When: OWD is set to Public Read Only or Private

Role Hierarchy Components:

  • Role: Named position in hierarchy (e.g., "VP Sales", "Sales Rep")
  • Level: Depth in the hierarchy tree
  • Parent-Child Relationship: Defines reporting structure
  • User Assignment: Each user assigned to one role

Example Hierarchy:

CEO
├── VP Sales
│   ├── Sales Manager West
│   │   ├── Sales Rep 1
│   │   └── Sales Rep 2
│   └── Sales Manager East
│       ├── Sales Rep 3
│       └── Sales Rep 4
└── VP Marketing
    ├── Marketing Manager
    │   ├── Marketing Specialist 1
    │   └── Marketing Specialist 2

Access Pattern:

// If OWD for Opportunities is Private:
// - Sales Rep 1 sees only their own opportunities
// - Sales Manager West sees opportunities for Rep 1 and Rep 2
// - VP Sales sees opportunities for all sales reps and managers
// - Marketing team sees no sales opportunities (different branch)

When to Use Role Hierarchy:

  • Use When: You have a clear management structure
  • Use When: Managers need to see subordinates' records
  • Use When: Data access follows organizational reporting structure
  • Use When: You want automatic record access based on position

When NOT to Use Role Hierarchy:

  • Don't Use: For flat organizations with no hierarchy
  • Don't Use: For complex matrix organizations
  • Don't Use: When access doesn't follow reporting structure
  • Alternative: Use Territory Management for geographic sales organizations

Configuration Steps:

  1. Setup → Users → Roles
  2. Click "Set Up Roles"
  3. Add roles starting from top of hierarchy
  4. Assign users to roles
  5. Set OWD to Private or Public Read Only for hierarchy to take effect

Role Settings:

Each Role Can Configure:
- Opportunity Access: "Read Only" or "Read/Write/Delete"
- Case Access: "Read Only" or "Read/Write/Delete"  
- Contact Access: "Read Only" or "Read/Write/Delete"
- Account/Territory Settings

Apex and Role Hierarchy:

// Query respects role hierarchy by default
// This returns records user can access via role hierarchy
List<Opportunity> opps = [
    SELECT Id, Name, Amount 
    FROM Opportunity 
    WHERE StageName = 'Closed Won'
];

// Bypass sharing (requires appropriate permissions)
// This ignores role hierarchy
List<Opportunity> allOpps = [
    SELECT Id, Name, Amount 
    FROM Opportunity 
    WHERE StageName = 'Closed Won'
    ALL ROWS
];

Role Hierarchy Optimization:

// Check if current user has access through role hierarchy
public static Boolean hasAccessThroughHierarchy(Id recordId) {
    // This query will only return record if user has access
    List<Account> accounts = [
        SELECT Id 
        FROM Account 
        WHERE Id = :recordId 
        LIMIT 1
    ];
    return !accounts.isEmpty();
}

Performance Considerations:

  • Deep hierarchies (10+ levels) can impact sharing calculations
  • Wide hierarchies (100+ roles at same level) are more performant
  • Role hierarchy changes trigger sharing recalculation

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Professional Edition and above
  • ❌ Not available in Essentials Edition
  • ✅ Available in all Enterprise, Unlimited, and Developer editions

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 500 roles per organization

⚠️ Role changes trigger sharing recalculation (can take time)

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Keep hierarchy as flat as possible (fewer levels = better performance)
  • ✅ Use descriptive role names (e.g., "Sales Manager - West Region")
  • ✅ Align roles with actual reporting structure
  • ✅ Don't create roles for every job title - focus on data access needs
  • ✅ Use "Grant Access Using Hierarchies" checkbox to enable/disable per object
  • ✅ Consider Territory Management for complex sales structures
  • ✅ Test sharing calculations after role hierarchy changes
  • ✅ Document role hierarchy structure and access patterns

Common Mistakes:

  • ❌ Creating too many roles (causes maintenance overhead)
  • ❌ Not aligning roles with actual business structure
  • ❌ Using role hierarchy when Territory Management is more appropriate
  • ❌ Forgetting that lateral users cannot see each other's records

See Also:

  • Territory Management (alternative for geographic organizations)
  • Sharing Rules (grants access across branches)
  • Grant Access Using Hierarchies setting (enable/disable per object)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What are Sharing Rules and when should I use them?
docs.text:
A: Sharing Rules are automated mechanisms to grant record access to users who wouldn't normally have access through OWD, role hierarchy, or ownership. They extend sharing beyond the organization-wide defaults.

Types of Sharing Rules:

  • Criteria-Based: Share records matching specific criteria with groups of users
  • Owner-Based: Share records owned by specific users/groups with other users/groups

Key Characteristics:

  • Can only open up access (never restrict)
  • Run automatically when conditions are met
  • Support up to 300 sharing rules per object
  • Recalculated when criteria changes or ownership changes

Criteria-Based Sharing Rule Example:

Rule Name: Share High Value Accounts with Sales Management
Object: Account
Criteria: Annual Revenue greater than $1,000,000
Share With: Public Group "Sales Managers"
Access Level: Read/Write

Owner-Based Sharing Rule Example:

Rule Name: Share West Region Opportunities with Sales Operations
Object: Opportunity
Owned By: Public Group "West Region Sales Reps"
Share With: Public Group "Sales Operations"
Access Level: Read Only

Configuration Steps:

  1. Setup → Security → Sharing Settings
  2. Find the object you want to share
  3. Click "New" in Sharing Rules section
  4. Select criteria-based or owner-based
  5. Define the criteria or owner conditions
  6. Select who to share with
  7. Set access level (Read Only or Read/Write)

Access Levels:

  • Read Only: View records only
  • Read/Write: View and edit records
  • Full Access: Available only for certain objects (Campaigns, Cases, Leads)

Sharing Rule Groups:

Valid Groups for Sharing Rules:
- Public Groups (manually maintained)
- Roles
- Roles and Subordinates (includes hierarchy below role)
- Territories
- Territories and Subordinates
- Queues (for Case and Lead sharing)

Complex Criteria Example:

// Apex trigger to manually share records based on complex logic
trigger AccountSharingTrigger on Account (after insert, after update) {
    List<AccountShare> sharesToInsert = new List<AccountShare>();

    // Get the group ID for Sales Operations
    Group salesOps = [
        SELECT Id 
        FROM Group 
        WHERE DeveloperName = 'Sales_Operations' 
        AND Type = 'Regular' 
        LIMIT 1
    ];

    for (Account acc : Trigger.new) {
        // Complex criteria: High value AND specific industry
        if (acc.AnnualRevenue > 1000000 && 
            acc.Industry == 'Technology' &&
            acc.Rating == 'Hot') {

            AccountShare share = new AccountShare();
            share.AccountId = acc.Id;
            share.UserOrGroupId = salesOps.Id;
            share.AccountAccessLevel = 'Edit';
            share.OpportunityAccessLevel = 'Edit';
            share.CaseAccessLevel = 'Edit';
            share.RowCause = Schema.AccountShare.RowCause.Manual;

            sharesToInsert.add(share);
        }
    }

    if (!sharesToInsert.isEmpty()) {
        Database.insert(sharesToInsert, false);
    }
}

Programmatic Sharing Example:

public class AccountSharingService {

    public static void shareAccountsWithExecutives(Set<Id> accountIds) {
        // Get Executive group
        Group executives = [
            SELECT Id 
            FROM Group 
            WHERE DeveloperName = 'Executive_Team' 
            LIMIT 1
        ];

        List<AccountShare> shares = new List<AccountShare>();

        for (Id accountId : accountIds) {
            AccountShare share = new AccountShare();
            share.AccountId = accountId;
            share.UserOrGroupId = executives.Id;
            share.AccountAccessLevel = 'Read';
            share.OpportunityAccessLevel = 'Read';
            share.RowCause = Schema.AccountShare.RowCause.Manual;

            shares.add(share);
        }

        try {
            Database.insert(shares, false);
        } catch (DmlException e) {
            System.debug('Sharing failed: ' + e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    public static void revokeAccountSharing(Set<Id> accountIds, Id groupId) {
        List<AccountShare> sharesToDelete = [
            SELECT Id 
            FROM AccountShare 
            WHERE AccountId IN :accountIds 
            AND UserOrGroupId = :groupId
            AND RowCause = :Schema.AccountShare.RowCause.Manual
        ];

        if (!sharesToDelete.isEmpty()) {
            delete sharesToDelete;
        }
    }
}

When to Use Sharing Rules:

  • Use When: Access doesn't follow role hierarchy
  • Use When: Cross-functional teams need access
  • Use When: Regional or product-based sharing is needed
  • Use When: Temporary project teams need access
  • Use When: Support teams need access to specific account types

When NOT to Use Sharing Rules:

  • Don't Use: When role hierarchy already provides access
  • Don't Use: For highly dynamic criteria (use Apex sharing instead)
  • Don't Use: When you're hitting the 300 rule limit (consolidate or use Apex)
  • Alternative: Use Territory Management for complex geographic structures

Sharing Rule Performance:

Performance Impact (from least to most):
1. Owner-Based Rules (fastest)
2. Criteria-Based Rules with indexed fields
3. Criteria-Based Rules with non-indexed fields (slowest)
4. Rules with multiple criteria (slower)
5. Rules using formula fields (slowest)

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Professional Edition and above
  • ✅ Criteria-based rules require Enterprise Edition or above
  • ❌ Not available in Essentials Edition

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 300 sharing rules per object

⚠️ Maximum 50 criteria per sharing rule

⚠️ Sharing recalculation time varies with data volume

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Use indexed fields in criteria-based rules for better performance
  • ✅ Consolidate similar rules when possible
  • ✅ Name rules clearly to indicate their purpose
  • ✅ Document business justification for each rule
  • ✅ Use Public Groups for flexibility (easier to modify membership)
  • ✅ Test sharing rules with actual user accounts
  • ✅ Monitor sharing rule calculation times
  • ✅ Use owner-based rules instead of criteria-based when possible
  • ✅ Consider Apex sharing for complex, dynamic requirements
  • ✅ Schedule regular audits of sharing rules

Common Mistakes:

  • ❌ Using non-indexed fields in criteria (causes performance issues)
  • ❌ Creating too many granular rules (consolidate instead)
  • ❌ Not considering parent object sharing for related records
  • ❌ Forgetting to share parent records when sharing child records

See Also:

  • Apex Managed Sharing (for complex dynamic sharing)
  • Territory Management (alternative for geographic sharing)
  • Manual Sharing (ad-hoc record sharing)
  • Implicit Sharing (automatic sharing for related records)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is Apex Managed Sharing and when should I implement it?
docs.text:
A: Apex Managed Sharing allows developers to programmatically grant record access using Apex code, providing fine-grained control beyond declarative sharing rules. It's ideal for complex, dynamic sharing scenarios that can't be handled with standard sharing rules.

Key Concepts:

  • Share Objects: Special objects (e.g., AccountShare, ContactShare) that store sharing records
  • RowCause: Identifies why a record is shared (must be a custom Apex sharing reason)
  • Programmatic Control: Sharing logic implemented in Apex triggers or scheduled jobs
  • Recalculation: Unlike declarative rules, Apex sharing doesn't auto-recalculate

Share Object Structure:

// AccountShare object fields
AccountShare share = new AccountShare();
share.AccountId = accountId;              // Record being shared
share.UserOrGroupId = userId;             // User or group getting access
share.AccountAccessLevel = 'Read';        // Access level: Read or Edit
share.OpportunityAccessLevel = 'Read';    // Access to related Opportunities
share.CaseAccessLevel = 'Read';           // Access to related Cases
share.RowCause = 'Manual';                // Why record is shared

Custom Apex Sharing Reason:

<!-- In Account.object-meta.xml -->
<sharingReasons>
    <sharingReason>
        <label>Special Project Access</label>
        <name>Special_Project</name>
    </sharingReason>
    <sharingReason>
        <label>Executive Review</label>
        <name>Executive_Review</name>
    </sharingReason>
</sharingReasons>

Complete Apex Sharing Implementation:

public class OpportunityTeamSharing {

    // Share opportunities with team members
    public static void shareWithTeamMembers(Set<Id> opportunityIds) {

        // Get opportunity team members
        List<OpportunityTeamMember> teamMembers = [
            SELECT Id, OpportunityId, UserId, TeamMemberRole
            FROM OpportunityTeamMember
            WHERE OpportunityId IN :opportunityIds
        ];

        List<OpportunityShare> sharesToInsert = new List<OpportunityShare>();
        Set<String> existingShares = new Set<String>();

        // Check existing shares to avoid duplicates
        List<OpportunityShare> existing = [
            SELECT OpportunityId, UserOrGroupId
            FROM OpportunityShare
            WHERE OpportunityId IN :opportunityIds
            AND RowCause = :Schema.OpportunityShare.RowCause.Team__c
        ];

        for (OpportunityShare share : existing) {
            existingShares.add(
                String.valueOf(share.OpportunityId) + '_' + 
                String.valueOf(share.UserOrGroupId)
            );
        }

        // Create sharing records for team members
        for (OpportunityTeamMember member : teamMembers) {
            String shareKey = String.valueOf(member.OpportunityId) + '_' + 
                            String.valueOf(member.UserId);

            if (!existingShares.contains(shareKey)) {
                OpportunityShare share = new OpportunityShare();
                share.OpportunityId = member.OpportunityId;
                share.UserOrGroupId = member.UserId;

                // Set access level based on role
                if (member.TeamMemberRole == 'Account Manager') {
                    share.OpportunityAccessLevel = 'Edit';
                } else {
                    share.OpportunityAccessLevel = 'Read';
                }

                share.RowCause = Schema.OpportunityShare.RowCause.Team__c;
                sharesToInsert.add(share);
            }
        }

        if (!sharesToInsert.isEmpty()) {
            Database.SaveResult[] results = Database.insert(sharesToInsert, false);

            // Handle errors
            for (Integer i = 0; i < results.size(); i++) {
                if (!results[i].isSuccess()) {
                    System.debug('Failed to share: ' + results[i].getErrors());
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // Remove sharing when team member is removed
    public static void removeTeamMemberAccess(Set<Id> opportunityIds, Set<Id> userIds) {
        List<OpportunityShare> sharesToDelete = [
            SELECT Id 
            FROM OpportunityShare 
            WHERE OpportunityId IN :opportunityIds 
            AND UserOrGroupId IN :userIds
            AND RowCause = :Schema.OpportunityShare.RowCause.Team__c
        ];

        if (!sharesToDelete.isEmpty()) {
            delete sharesToDelete;
        }
    }

    // Recalculate all sharing (use sparingly)
    public static void recalculateSharing(Set<Id> opportunityIds) {
        // First remove all existing Apex managed shares
        delete [
            SELECT Id 
            FROM OpportunityShare 
            WHERE OpportunityId IN :opportunityIds
            AND RowCause = :Schema.OpportunityShare.RowCause.Team__c
        ];

        // Then recreate shares
        shareWithTeamMembers(opportunityIds);
    }
}

Trigger Implementation:

trigger OpportunityTeamSharingTrigger on OpportunityTeamMember (
    after insert, after update, after delete
) {
    Set<Id> opportunityIds = new Set<Id>();
    Set<Id> userIdsToRemove = new Set<Id>();

    if (Trigger.isDelete) {
        for (OpportunityTeamMember member : Trigger.old) {
            opportunityIds.add(member.OpportunityId);
            userIdsToRemove.add(member.UserId);
        }
        OpportunityTeamSharing.removeTeamMemberAccess(
            opportunityIds, 
            userIdsToRemove
        );
    } else {
        for (OpportunityTeamMember member : Trigger.new) {
            opportunityIds.add(member.OpportunityId);
        }
        OpportunityTeamSharing.shareWithTeamMembers(opportunityIds);
    }
}

Batch Apex for Recalculation:

public class RecalculateSharingBatch implements Database.Batchable<sObject> {

    private String objectName;
    private String rowCause;

    public RecalculateSharingBatch(String objectName, String rowCause) {
        this.objectName = objectName;
        this.rowCause = rowCause;
    }

    public Database.QueryLocator start(Database.BatchableContext bc) {
        String query = 'SELECT Id FROM ' + objectName;
        return Database.getQueryLocator(query);
    }

    public void execute(Database.BatchableContext bc, List<sObject> scope) {
        Set<Id> recordIds = new Set<Id>();
        for (sObject record : scope) {
            recordIds.add(record.Id);
        }

        // Delete existing Apex managed shares
        String shareObjectName = objectName + 'Share';
        String deleteQuery = 'SELECT Id FROM ' + shareObjectName + 
                           ' WHERE ' + objectName + 'Id IN :recordIds' +
                           ' AND RowCause = :rowCause';
        List<sObject> sharesToDelete = Database.query(deleteQuery);
        delete sharesToDelete;

        // Recreate shares based on custom logic
        // Implementation depends on your sharing requirements
    }

    public void finish(Database.BatchableContext bc) {
        System.debug('Sharing recalculation complete');
    }
}

When to Use Apex Managed Sharing:

  • Use When: Sharing criteria is too complex for declarative rules
  • Use When: Sharing depends on data from multiple objects
  • Use When: You've hit the 300 sharing rule limit
  • Use When: Sharing needs to change dynamically based on record updates
  • Use When: You need conditional sharing logic based on user attributes

When NOT to Use Apex Managed Sharing:

  • Don't Use: When declarative rules can handle the requirement
  • Don't Use: For simple owner-based or criteria-based sharing
  • Don't Use: If you're not comfortable managing sharing recalculation
  • Alternative: Use standard sharing rules when possible

Performance Considerations:

// Efficient: Bulk sharing operations
List<AccountShare> shares = new List<AccountShare>();
for (Account acc : accounts) {
    // Create share records
}
insert shares;

// Inefficient: DML in loops
for (Account acc : accounts) {
    AccountShare share = new AccountShare();
    // ... set fields ...
    insert share;  // ❌ DML in loop
}

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Enterprise Edition and above
  • ✅ Unlimited Edition
  • ✅ Developer Edition
  • ❌ Not available in Professional or Essentials Edition

Governor Limits:

⚠️ 150 DML statements per transaction (includes share record inserts)

⚠️ 10,000 records per DML statement

⚠️ Share object queries count toward SOQL limit (100 per transaction)

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Always bulkify sharing operations
  • ✅ Check for existing shares before inserting to avoid duplicates
  • ✅ Use custom Apex sharing reasons to identify your shares
  • ✅ Implement error handling for sharing failures
  • ✅ Create a recalculation mechanism for data fixes
  • ✅ Document sharing logic thoroughly
  • ✅ Test with large data volumes
  • ✅ Monitor sharing record volume growth
  • ✅ Consider asynchronous processing for large-scale updates
  • ✅ Use Database.insert(records, false) to handle partial failures

Common Mistakes:

  • ❌ Not handling duplicate share records (causes exceptions)
  • ❌ DML operations in loops
  • ❌ Not providing a way to recalculate sharing
  • ❌ Forgetting to remove shares when conditions change
  • ❌ Not testing with different user profiles
  • ❌ Creating too many share records (performance impact)

Test Class Example:

@isTest
private class OpportunityTeamSharingTest {

    @testSetup
    static void setup() {
        // Create test data
        Account acc = new Account(Name = 'Test Account');
        insert acc;

        Opportunity opp = new Opportunity(
            Name = 'Test Opp',
            AccountId = acc.Id,
            StageName = 'Prospecting',
            CloseDate = Date.today().addDays(30)
        );
        insert opp;
    }

    @isTest
    static void testTeamMemberSharing() {
        Opportunity opp = [SELECT Id FROM Opportunity LIMIT 1];
        User testUser = [SELECT Id FROM User WHERE Profile.Name = 'Standard User' LIMIT 1];

        Test.startTest();

        // Add team member
        OpportunityTeamMember member = new OpportunityTeamMember(
            OpportunityId = opp.Id,
            UserId = testUser.Id,
            TeamMemberRole = 'Account Manager'
        );
        insert member;

        Test.stopTest();

        // Verify sharing was created
        List<OpportunityShare> shares = [
            SELECT Id, OpportunityAccessLevel
            FROM OpportunityShare
            WHERE OpportunityId = :opp.Id
            AND UserOrGroupId = :testUser.Id
            AND RowCause = :Schema.OpportunityShare.RowCause.Team__c
        ];

        System.assertEquals(1, shares.size(), 'Share record should be created');
        System.assertEquals('Edit', shares[0].OpportunityAccessLevel, 
                          'Account Manager should have edit access');
    }
}

See Also:

  • Share Objects (AccountShare, OpportunityShare, etc.)
  • Database.insert with allOrNone parameter
  • Apex Sharing Reasons (custom reasons)
  • Asynchronous Apex for large-scale sharing updates

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What are Permission Set Groups and how do they differ from Permission Sets?
docs.text:
A: Permission Set Groups are containers that bundle multiple permission sets together, allowing administrators to assign a collection of permissions to users with a single assignment rather than assigning permission sets individually.

Key Differences:

  • Permission Set: Individual collection of permissions
  • Permission Set Group: Bundle of multiple permission sets assigned as a unit
  • Permission Set: Can be assigned directly to users
  • Permission Set Group: Assigns all contained permission sets at once

Permission Set Group Components:

Permission Set Group: "Sales Manager Access"
├── Permission Set: "Account Management"
├── Permission Set: "Opportunity Management"  
├── Permission Set: "Report Builder"
└── Permission Set: "Dashboard Viewer"

When to Use Permission Set Groups:

  • Use When: Users need multiple related permission sets
  • Use When: You want to standardize permission combinations
  • Use When: Onboarding new users with consistent access
  • Use When: Managing role-based access control (RBAC)
  • Use When: Simplifying permission set administration

Configuration Steps:

  1. Setup → Users → Permission Set Groups
  2. Click "New Permission Set Group"
  3. Enter name and description
  4. Add permission sets to the group
  5. Assign the group to users

Muting Permission Sets:

Feature: Muting Permission Sets
Purpose: Temporarily remove specific permissions from a group member

Example:
Permission Set Group: "Sales Manager Access"
- Contains: Account Management (Edit access)
- User needs temporary read-only access
- Solution: Add "Mute Account Edit" permission set
- Result: Edit permission temporarily removed

Programmatic Assignment:

// Assign Permission Set Group to user
public static void assignPermissionSetGroup(Id userId, String groupName) {
    // Get Permission Set Group
    PermissionSetGroup psg = [
        SELECT Id 
        FROM PermissionSetGroup 
        WHERE DeveloperName = :groupName 
        LIMIT 1
    ];

    // Check if already assigned
    List<PermissionSetAssignment> existing = [
        SELECT Id 
        FROM PermissionSetAssignment 
        WHERE AssigneeId = :userId 
        AND PermissionSetGroupId = :psg.Id
    ];

    if (existing.isEmpty()) {
        PermissionSetAssignment psa = new PermissionSetAssignment(
            AssigneeId = userId,
            PermissionSetGroupId = psg.Id
        );
        insert psa;
    }
}

// Remove Permission Set Group from user
public static void removePermissionSetGroup(Id userId, String groupName) {
    PermissionSetGroup psg = [
        SELECT Id 
        FROM PermissionSetGroup 
        WHERE DeveloperName = :groupName 
        LIMIT 1
    ];

    List<PermissionSetAssignment> assignments = [
        SELECT Id 
        FROM PermissionSetAssignment 
        WHERE AssigneeId = :userId 
        AND PermissionSetGroupId = :psg.Id
    ];

    if (!assignments.isEmpty()) {
        delete assignments;
    }
}

Permission Set Group Architecture:

public class PermissionManager {

    // Get all permission sets in a group
    public static List<PermissionSet> getPermissionSetsInGroup(String groupName) {
        PermissionSetGroup psg = [
            SELECT Id, (
                SELECT PermissionSetId, PermissionSet.Name 
                FROM PermissionSetGroupComponents
            )
            FROM PermissionSetGroup 
            WHERE DeveloperName = :groupName 
            LIMIT 1
        ];

        Set<Id> permSetIds = new Set<Id>();
        for (PermissionSetGroupComponent comp : psg.PermissionSetGroupComponents) {
            permSetIds.add(comp.PermissionSetId);
        }

        return [SELECT Id, Name, Label FROM PermissionSet WHERE Id IN :permSetIds];
    }

    // Check if user has permission set group
    public static Boolean userHasGroup(Id userId, String groupName) {
        Integer count = [
            SELECT COUNT()
            FROM PermissionSetAssignment
            WHERE AssigneeId = :userId
            AND PermissionSetGroup.DeveloperName = :groupName
        ];
        return count > 0;
    }

    // Get all groups assigned to user
    public static List<PermissionSetGroup> getUserGroups(Id userId) {
        List<PermissionSetAssignment> assignments = [
            SELECT PermissionSetGroup.Id, PermissionSetGroup.MasterLabel
            FROM PermissionSetAssignment
            WHERE AssigneeId = :userId
            AND PermissionSetGroupId != null
        ];

        Set<Id> groupIds = new Set<Id>();
        for (PermissionSetAssignment psa : assignments) {
            groupIds.add(psa.PermissionSetGroup.Id);
        }

        return [
            SELECT Id, MasterLabel, DeveloperName 
            FROM PermissionSetGroup 
            WHERE Id IN :groupIds
        ];
    }
}

Best Practices for Organization:

Recommended Permission Set Group Structure:

By Role:
- "Sales Representative"
  └── Base sales permissions
- "Sales Manager"  
  └── Sales rep permissions + management tools
- "Sales Director"
  └── Manager permissions + executive reports

By Function:
- "API Integration User"
  └── API access + integration permissions
- "Report Administrator"
  └── Report creation + dashboard management
- "Data Administrator"
  └── Data import/export + mass operations

By Project:
- "Q1 Product Launch Team"
  └── Temporary project-specific access
- "GDPR Compliance Team"
  └── Privacy and data management tools

Comparison Table:

| Feature                    | Permission Set | Permission Set Group |
|---------------------------|----------------|----------------------|
| Contains permissions       | ✅ Yes         | ❌ No (contains PSs)  |
| Can be assigned to users   | ✅ Yes         | ✅ Yes                |
| Can contain other items    | ❌ No          | ✅ Yes (PSs)          |
| Supports muting            | ❌ No          | ✅ Yes                |
| Assignment limit per user  | 1,500          | Part of 1,500 limit  |

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Enterprise Edition and above
  • ✅ Unlimited Edition
  • ✅ Developer Edition
  • ❌ Not available in Professional or Essentials Edition

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 1,000 permission set groups per org

⚠️ Maximum 100 permission sets per group

⚠️ Maximum 1,500 total permission set assignments per user (includes groups)

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Use groups to standardize permission combinations
  • ✅ Name groups clearly based on role or function
  • ✅ Document which permission sets are in each group
  • ✅ Use muting permission sets for temporary access changes
  • ✅ Assign groups instead of individual permission sets
  • ✅ Create groups for common role-based access patterns
  • ✅ Review group membership quarterly
  • ✅ Test groups with actual user accounts before deployment

Common Mistakes:

  • ❌ Creating too many overlapping groups
  • ❌ Not documenting the purpose of each group
  • ❌ Mixing unrelated permissions in one group
  • ❌ Not using muting permission sets when needed
  • ❌ Assigning individual permission sets when a group exists

Migration Strategy:

Moving from Individual Permission Sets to Groups:

1. Audit Current State
   - Document all permission set assignments
   - Identify common permission set combinations

2. Design Groups
   - Group permission sets by role/function
   - Name groups descriptively

3. Create Groups
   - Build permission set groups
   - Test with pilot users

4. Migrate Users
   - Assign groups to users
   - Remove individual permission set assignments
   - Verify access hasn't changed

5. Maintain
   - Add new permission sets to appropriate groups
   - Review group membership regularly

See Also:

  • Permission Sets (individual collections of permissions)
  • Muting Permission Sets (temporary permission removal)
  • Session-Based Permission Set Groups (temporary group access)

docs.title: Q: How do I implement Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) in Salesforce?
docs.text:
A: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) adds an extra layer of security by requiring users to provide two forms of identification: their password (something they know) and a verification code (something they have). Salesforce supports multiple 2FA methods to protect user accounts.

Available 2FA Methods:

  • Salesforce Authenticator App: Mobile app that generates verification codes and sends push notifications
  • Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP): Third-party authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator)
  • Security Key (U2F/WebAuthn): Physical security keys like YubiKey
  • Built-in Authenticator: Salesforce's built-in authenticator for mobile devices

When 2FA is Required:

  • UI Logins: Access through browser to Salesforce org
  • API Connections: Can be exempt if using connected apps with proper security
  • Mobile Access: Salesforce mobile app logins
  • Community Access: Community and Experience Cloud users (if enabled)

Implementation Steps:

Step 1: Enable Multi-Factor Authentication

  1. Setup → Identity → Multi-Factor Authentication
  2. Enable "Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all direct UI logins to your Salesforce org"
  3. Set effective date for rollout

Step 2: Configure Authentication Methods

  1. Setup → Session Settings
  2. Enable desired authentication methods:
  3. Salesforce Authenticator
  4. Time-based one-time passwords (TOTP)
  5. Universal Second Factor (U2F) security keys

Step 3: User Registration

User Self-Registration Process:

1. User logs in with username and password
2. Salesforce prompts to register authenticator
3. User selects preferred method:
   - Downloads Salesforce Authenticator app
   - OR scans QR code with TOTP app
   - OR plugs in security key
4. User completes registration
5. Future logins require password + 2FA

Programmatic 2FA Management:

// Check if user has MFA enabled
public static Boolean isMFAEnabled(Id userId) {
    User u = [
        SELECT Id, Name, 
        (SELECT Id FROM TwoFactorInfo LIMIT 1)
        FROM User 
        WHERE Id = :userId
    ];
    return !u.TwoFactorInfo.isEmpty();
}

// Get MFA methods registered for user
public static List<String> getUserMFAMethods(Id userId) {
    List<String> methods = new List<String>();

    List<TwoFactorInfo> mfaRecords = [
        SELECT Id, Type 
        FROM TwoFactorInfo 
        WHERE UserId = :userId
    ];

    for (TwoFactorInfo tfi : mfaRecords) {
        methods.add(tfi.Type);
    }

    return methods;
}

// Disable user's MFA (admin only, requires session-based permission)
public static void removeMFAForUser(Id userId) {
    List<TwoFactorInfo> toDelete = [
        SELECT Id 
        FROM TwoFactorInfo 
        WHERE UserId = :userId
    ];

    if (!toDelete.isEmpty()) {
        delete toDelete;
    }
}

Connected App Configuration for API Access:

<!-- Connected App Settings -->
<ConnectedApp>
    <oauthConfig>
        <policies>
            <!-- Relax IP restrictions for API users -->
            <ipRelaxation>RELAX_IP</ipRelaxation>

            <!-- Refresh token policy -->
            <refreshTokenPolicy>REFRESH_TOKEN_REVOKE_ON_RENEWAL</refreshTokenPolicy>
        </policies>

        <!-- Permitted Users -->
        <permittedUsers>ADMIN_APPROVED</permittedUsers>
    </oauthConfig>
</ConnectedApp>

API Access with 2FA:

// OAuth 2.0 flow for API access (bypasses direct UI 2FA requirement)
public class SalesforceAPIConnection {

    private String clientId;
    private String clientSecret;
    private String username;
    private String password;
    private String securityToken;

    public String getAccessToken() {
        HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest();
        req.setEndpoint('https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token');
        req.setMethod('POST');

        String body = 'grant_type=password';
        body += '&client_id=' + clientId;
        body += '&client_secret=' + clientSecret;
        body += '&username=' + username;
        body += '&password=' + password + securityToken;

        req.setBody(body);

        Http http = new Http();
        HttpResponse res = http.send(req);

        if (res.getStatusCode() == 200) {
            Map<String, Object> response = 
                (Map<String, Object>) JSON.deserializeUntyped(res.getBody());
            return (String) response.get('access_token');
        }

        return null;
    }
}

Session-Based MFA Permissions:

// Grant temporary MFA permission
public class SessionMFAManager {

    public static void grantTemporaryMFAAccess(Id userId) {
        // Create session-based permission set assignment
        SessionPermSet sps = new SessionPermSet();
        sps.UserId = userId;
        sps.SessionLevel = 'HIGH_ASSURANCE';
        // Additional configuration as needed

        // Note: Actual implementation depends on org setup
    }
}

User Experience Considerations:

Registration Methods by User Preference:

Tech-Savvy Users:
- ✅ TOTP authenticator apps (Google, Microsoft)
- ✅ Security keys for fastest login

Mobile-First Users:
- ✅ Salesforce Authenticator (push notifications)
- ✅ Built-in authenticator on iOS/Android

Security-Conscious Users:
- ✅ Physical security keys (YubiKey)
- ✅ Multiple backup methods registered

Troubleshooting Common Issues:

Issue: User lost phone with authenticator
Solution: 
1. Admin goes to Setup → Users
2. Find user → Reset Security Token
3. User registers new device

Issue: User can't receive push notifications
Solution:
1. Check phone settings for app notifications
2. Ensure phone has internet connectivity
3. Re-register Salesforce Authenticator app

Issue: API integration failing after 2FA
Solution:
1. Use Connected App with OAuth
2. Configure IP relaxation policies
3. Use integration user with API-only profile

Exempting Users from UI 2FA:

Use Cases for Exemption:
- API-only users (use API authentication instead)
- Integration users (use connected apps)
- Temporary access (use session-based permission sets)

How to Exempt:
1. Create Permission Set: "MFA Not Required"
2. Assign to specific users
3. Monitor usage carefully (security risk!)

⚠️ WARNING: Exemptions reduce security - use sparingly

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Available in all editions (some features vary)
  • ✅ Salesforce Authenticator available in all editions
  • ✅ Security keys available in all editions
  • ✅ TOTP authenticators available in all editions

Compliance Requirements:

2FA Required for Compliance:
- ✅ SOC 2 Type II
- ✅ HIPAA (healthcare)
- ✅ PCI DSS (payment card industry)
- ✅ GDPR (data protection)
- ✅ ISO 27001

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Enable 2FA for all users, especially admins
  • ✅ Allow multiple authentication methods for user flexibility
  • ✅ Require registration within 7 days of rollout
  • ✅ Provide clear documentation and training
  • ✅ Set up help desk procedures for lost devices
  • ✅ Use connected apps for API integrations
  • ✅ Monitor failed authentication attempts
  • ✅ Regularly audit 2FA registration compliance
  • ✅ Register backup authentication methods
  • ✅ Test 2FA process before organization-wide rollout

Common Mistakes:

  • ❌ Enabling 2FA without user training
  • ❌ Not having a process for lost devices
  • ❌ Breaking API integrations by not configuring connected apps
  • ❌ Not registering backup authentication methods
  • ❌ Exempting too many users from 2FA requirements

Rollout Strategy:

Phase 1: Pilot (2 weeks)
- Enable for IT team and power users
- Gather feedback
- Refine documentation

Phase 2: Admins and Developers (1 week)
- Enable for all admins
- Enable for all developers
- Monitor support requests

Phase 3: Phased Rollout (4 weeks)
- Week 1: Executive team
- Week 2: Department heads
- Week 3: General users (Group 1)
- Week 4: General users (Group 2)

Phase 4: Enforcement
- Enable mandatory requirement
- Monitor compliance
- Handle exceptions

See Also:

  • Connected Apps (for API access)
  • Session Security (session-based permissions)
  • Security Token (for API authentication)
  • Login Flows (custom authentication flows)

docs.title: Q: What is Shield Platform Encryption and when should I use it?
docs.text:
A: Shield Platform Encryption is an advanced security feature that encrypts data at rest at the application layer using a customer-controlled encryption key. Unlike standard encryption, Shield encryption protects sensitive data with keys that customers can manage and rotate.

Key Concepts:

  • Data at Rest: Encrypts stored data in Salesforce databases
  • Application-Layer Encryption: Encrypts before data is written to database
  • Customer-Managed Keys: Organizations can bring their own encryption keys
  • Key Hierarchy: Tenant secret, master secret, and data encryption keys
  • Field-Level Encryption: Encrypt specific fields on standard and custom objects

Standard vs Shield Encryption:

| Feature                          | Standard Encryption | Shield Platform Encryption |
|---------------------------------|---------------------|---------------------------|
| Data encrypted at rest          | ✅ Yes              | ✅ Yes                     |
| Salesforce-managed keys         | ✅ Yes              | ✅ Yes (option)            |
| Customer-managed keys (BYOK)    | ❌ No               | ✅ Yes                     |
| Field-level encryption          | ❌ No               | ✅ Yes                     |
| Files and attachments           | ❌ Limited          | ✅ Yes                     |
| Search encrypted data           | ✅ Full text        | ⚠️ Limited (deterministic) |
| External key management         | ❌ No               | ✅ Yes                     |

Encryption Schemes:

  • Probabilistic Encryption: Most secure, different ciphertext for same input, no search/filter/sort
  • Deterministic Encryption: Same ciphertext for same input, allows search/filter/exact match
  • Case-Insensitive Deterministic: Deterministic with case-insensitive matching

What Can Be Encrypted:

Supported Data Types for Encryption:
- ✅ Text fields (String, Email, Phone, URL)
- ✅ Number fields (Integer, Currency, Percent)
- ✅ Date and DateTime fields
- ✅ Attachments and Files
- ✅ Content in Salesforce Files
- ✅ Search index entries
- ❌ Formula fields (cannot encrypt directly)
- ❌ Lookup fields
- ❌ Geolocation fields

Configuration Steps:

Step 1: Purchase and Enable Shield

  1. Contact Salesforce to purchase Shield
  2. Setup → Platform Encryption → Get Started
  3. Generate tenant secret

Step 2: Encrypt Fields

  1. Setup → Platform Encryption → Encryption Policy
  2. Select object and fields to encrypt
  3. Choose encryption scheme
  4. Save and deploy

Step 3: Key Management

Key Management Options:

Salesforce-Managed (Default):
- Salesforce generates and stores keys
- Automatic key rotation
- Simplest option

Bring Your Own Key (BYOK):
- Upload your own tenant secret
- Customer controls key lifecycle
- Requires key management infrastructure

Apex Examples:

// Check if field is encrypted
public static Boolean isFieldEncrypted(String objectName, String fieldName) {
    Schema.SObjectType objectType = Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(objectName);
    Schema.DescribeSObjectResult describeResult = objectType.getDescribe();
    Schema.DescribeFieldResult fieldResult = 
        describeResult.fields.getMap().get(fieldName).getDescribe();

    return fieldResult.isEncrypted();
}

// Query encrypted fields (works normally in Apex)
public static List<Contact> getEncryptedContacts() {
    // SSN field is encrypted with Shield
    List<Contact> contacts = [
        SELECT Id, Name, SSN__c, Email
        FROM Contact
        WHERE SSN__c != null
        LIMIT 100
    ];

    // Data is automatically decrypted for authorized users
    return contacts;
}

// Deterministic encryption allows filtering
public static List<Contact> searchByEncryptedSSN(String ssn) {
    // Only works if SSN__c uses deterministic encryption
    List<Contact> contacts = [
        SELECT Id, Name, SSN__c
        FROM Contact
        WHERE SSN__c = :ssn
    ];

    return contacts;
}

Key Rotation Process:

public class EncryptionKeyRotation {

    // Check key rotation status
    public static void checkRotationStatus() {
        // Query encryption key metadata
        List<TenantSecret> keys = [
            SELECT Id, Status, Type, CreatedDate
            FROM TenantSecret
            ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC
        ];

        for (TenantSecret key : keys) {
            System.debug('Key Status: ' + key.Status);
            System.debug('Key Type: ' + key.Type);
        }
    }

    // Archive old keys after rotation (admin operation)
    public static void archiveOldKeys() {
        // This is typically done through UI:
        // Setup → Platform Encryption → Key Management → Archive

        // Programmatic key management requires special permissions
    }
}

Performance Considerations:

Shield Encryption Performance Impact:

Query Performance:
- Probabilistic: No filtering/sorting (full table scans)
- Deterministic: Filtering allowed, slight overhead
- Standard fields: No impact on non-encrypted fields

CPU Impact:
- Encryption/Decryption uses CPU time
- Factor in governor limits for CPU time
- Consider for high-volume operations

Storage:
- Encrypted fields require more storage space
- Plan for 20-30% storage increase

Search:
- Full-text search limited on encrypted fields
- Use deterministic for search requirements

Compliance Use Cases:

Industries Requiring Shield Encryption:

Healthcare (HIPAA):
- Encrypt PHI (Protected Health Information)
- Patient medical records
- Billing information

Financial Services:
- Credit card numbers (PCI DSS)
- Bank account information
- Social Security Numbers

Government (FedRAMP):
- Classified information
- Citizen personal data
- Government contracts

European Union (GDPR):
- Personal identifiable information (PII)
- Employee data
- Customer data

BYOK Implementation:

public class BYOKManager {

    // Upload customer-provided encryption key
    public static void uploadTenantSecret(String keyMaterial) {
        // This operation requires Platform Encryption Administrator
        // Typically done through Setup UI, not Apex

        // Steps:
        // 1. Generate 256-bit AES key
        // 2. Wrap key using Salesforce public certificate
        // 3. Upload wrapped key to Salesforce
        // 4. Salesforce validates and activates key
    }

    // Key rotation schedule
    public static void scheduleKeyRotation() {
        // Best practice: Rotate keys every 12 months
        // Set up reminder workflow:
        // - 90 days before expiration: Plan rotation
        // - 30 days before: Test rotation in sandbox
        // - Day of: Execute rotation in production
    }
}

Backup and Disaster Recovery:

Shield Encryption Backup Considerations:

Data Exports:
- ✅ Encrypted data included in exports
- ✅ Data remains encrypted in export files
- ⚠️ Keys NOT included in exports

Restore Process:
- Load data back into Salesforce
- Encryption keys must be available
- Data automatically re-encrypted

Key Backup:
- Store tenant secret securely offline
- Use hardware security module (HSM)
- Multiple authorized personnel for key access

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Shield Platform Encryption add-on required
  • ✅ Available for Enterprise, Unlimited, and Performance editions
  • ❌ Not available in Professional, Essentials, or Developer editions
  • ✅ Separate licensing from Event Monitoring and Field Audit Trail

Governor Limits:

⚠️ CPU time impact from encryption/decryption operations

⚠️ No specific encryption field limits, but consider performance

⚠️ Storage overhead (20-30% increase)

Best Practices:

  • ✅ Encrypt only truly sensitive fields (minimize performance impact)
  • ✅ Use deterministic encryption for fields requiring search/filter
  • ✅ Test encryption in sandbox before production deployment
  • ✅ Document which fields are encrypted and why
  • ✅ Implement key rotation policy (annually minimum)
  • ✅ Backup tenant secret securely
  • ✅ Train users on encrypted field limitations
  • ✅ Use BYOK for maximum control over keys
  • ✅ Monitor encryption key expiration dates
  • ✅ Consider archive encryption for historical data

Common Mistakes:

  • ❌ Encrypting too many fields (performance impact)
  • ❌ Using probabilistic encryption when search is required
  • ❌ Not testing search and filter functionality after encryption
  • ❌ Not backing up encryption keys
  • ❌ Enabling encryption without understanding limitations
  • ❌ Not planning for key rotation

Migration Strategy:

Encrypting Existing Data:

Phase 1: Planning
- Identify sensitive fields
- Choose encryption scheme
- Test in sandbox

Phase 2: Encryption Rollout
- Enable encryption on new/updated records
- Schedule batch job to encrypt existing records
- Monitor progress

Phase 3: Validation
- Verify all records encrypted
- Test search/filter functionality
- Train users on changes

Phase 4: Ongoing Management
- Schedule key rotation
- Monitor performance
- Regular compliance audits

See Also:

  • Classic Encryption (field encryption for specific use cases)
  • Event Monitoring (audit encrypted field access)
  • Field Audit Trail (track changes to encrypted fields)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is Event Monitoring and how do I use it for security auditing?
docs.text:
A: Event Monitoring (part of Salesforce Shield) provides detailed tracking and analysis of user activity in your Salesforce org. It captures system performance data and security events in log files that can be downloaded and analyzed for security auditing, performance optimization, and compliance.

What Event Monitoring Captures:

  • Login Events: Successful and failed login attempts, session information
  • API Calls: REST, SOAP, Bulk API usage patterns
  • Report Executions: Who ran which reports and when
  • Dashboard Views: Dashboard access and refresh frequency
  • Document Downloads: File and attachment downloads
  • URI Events: Page views and navigation patterns
  • SOQL Queries: Queries executed, performance metrics
  • Apex Executions: Apex class and trigger executions

Event Types:

Security-Focused Events:
- Login (Login attempts and session details)
- LoginAs (Admin login as another user)
- Logout (Session terminations)
- CredentialStuffing (Suspicious login patterns)
- Session Hijacking Detection

Performance Events:
- API usage patterns
- Report runtime metrics
- Dashboard load times
- Apex CPU usage

Data Access Events:
- Report exports
- List views
- Bulk API queries
- Document downloads

Accessing Event Log Files:

// Query EventLogFile object to get log files
public class EventMonitoringService {

    // Get login event logs for last 24 hours
    public static List<EventLogFile> getLoginLogs() {
        DateTime yesterday = DateTime.now().addDays(-1);

        List<EventLogFile> logs = [
            SELECT Id, EventType, LogDate, LogFile, LogFileLength
            FROM EventLogFile
            WHERE EventType = 'Login'
            AND LogDate >= :yesterday
            ORDER BY LogDate DESC
        ];

        return logs;
    }

    // Download and parse log file content
    public static String getLogFileContent(Id logFileId) {
        EventLogFile logFile = [
            SELECT LogFile 
            FROM EventLogFile 
            WHERE Id = :logFileId
        ];

        // LogFile is a ContentVersion, need to query the file
        ContentVersion cv = [
            SELECT VersionData 
            FROM ContentVersion 
            WHERE Id = :logFile.LogFile
        ];

        Blob fileData = cv.VersionData;
        String csvContent = fileData.toString();

        return csvContent;
    }

    // Parse CSV log data
    public static List<Map<String, String>> parseLogFile(String csvContent) {
        List<Map<String, String>> records = new List<Map<String, String>>();
        List<String> lines = csvContent.split('\n');

        if (lines.isEmpty()) return records;

        // First line is header
        List<String> headers = lines[0].split(',');

        // Parse data rows
        for (Integer i = 1; i < lines.size(); i++) {
            List<String> values = lines[i].split(',');
            Map<String, String> record = new Map<String, String>();

            for (Integer j = 0; j < headers.size(); j++) {
                if (j < values.size()) {
                    record.put(headers[j], values[j]);
                }
            }
            records.add(record);
        }

        return records;
    }
}

Analyzing Failed Login Attempts:

public class SecurityAnalyzer {

    // Detect potential brute force attacks
    public static List<String> detectBruteForceAttempts() {
        List<String> suspiciousUsers = new List<String>();

        // Get recent login event logs
        List<EventLogFile> logs = EventMonitoringService.getLoginLogs();

        Map<String, Integer> failedAttempts = new Map<String, Integer>();

        for (EventLogFile log : logs) {
            String content = EventMonitoringService.getLogFileContent(log.Id);
            List<Map<String, String>> records = 
                EventMonitoringService.parseLogFile(content);

            for (Map<String, String> record : records) {
                String username = record.get('USER_NAME');
                String status = record.get('LOGIN_STATUS');

                if (status == 'LOGIN_INVALID_PASSWORD' || 
                    status == 'LOGIN_CHALLENGE_FAILED') {

                    Integer count = failedAttempts.get(username);
                    count = (count == null) ? 1 : count + 1;
                    failedAttempts.put(username, count);

                    // Alert if more than 5 failed attempts
                    if (count > 5) {
                        suspiciousUsers.add(username);
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        return suspiciousUsers;
    }

    // Track unusual access patterns
    public static void detectAnomalousAccess() {
        // Get login logs
        List<EventLogFile> logs = [
            SELECT Id, EventType 
            FROM EventLogFile 
            WHERE EventType = 'Login'
            AND LogDate = TODAY
        ];

        Map<String, Set<String>> userAccessPatterns = 
            new Map<String, Set<String>>();

        for (EventLogFile log : logs) {
            String content = EventMonitoringService.getLogFileContent(log.Id);
            List<Map<String, String>> records = 
                EventMonitoringService.parseLogFile(content);

            for (Map<String, String> record : records) {
                String username = record.get('USER_NAME');
                String sourceIp = record.get('SOURCE_IP');
                String loginTime = record.get('TIMESTAMP');

                // Track IP addresses per user
                if (!userAccessPatterns.containsKey(username)) {
                    userAccessPatterns.put(username, new Set<String>());
                }
                userAccessPatterns.get(username).add(sourceIp);

                // Alert if user logs in from more than 3 different IPs in one day
                if (userAccessPatterns.get(username).size() > 3) {
                    sendSecurityAlert(username, userAccessPatterns.get(username));
                }
            }
        }
    }

    private static void sendSecurityAlert(String username, Set<String> ips) {
        // Send alert email or create case
        System.debug('Security Alert: User ' + username + 
                    ' logged in from multiple IPs: ' + ips);
    }
}

Transaction Security Policies:

// Create custom transaction security policy
public class SuspiciousLoginPolicy implements TxnSecurity.PolicyCondition {

    public boolean evaluate(TxnSecurity.Event e) {
        // Access login event data
        LoginEvent loginEvent = (LoginEvent) e.data;

        // Check for suspicious patterns
        Boolean suspiciousLocation = checkLocationRisk(loginEvent.SourceIp);
        Boolean unusualTime = checkUnusualLoginTime(loginEvent.EventDate);
        Boolean newDevice = checkNewDevice(loginEvent.LoginKey);

        // Block if multiple risk factors present
        return (suspiciousLocation && unusualTime) || newDevice;
    }

    private Boolean checkLocationRisk(String sourceIp) {
        // Check if IP is from high-risk country
        // Implementation depends on IP geolocation service
        return false;
    }

    private Boolean checkUnusualLoginTime(DateTime loginTime) {
        // Check if login is outside normal business hours
        Time loginHour = loginTime.time();
        Time businessStart = Time.newInstance(8, 0, 0, 0);
        Time businessEnd = Time.newInstance(18, 0, 0, 0);

        return loginHour < businessStart || loginHour > businessEnd;
    }

    private Boolean checkNewDevice(String loginKey) {
        // Check if this is a new device for the user
        // Query login history
        return false;
    }
}

Real-Time Event Monitoring:

// Subscribe to platform events for real-time monitoring
public class RealtimeSecurityMonitor {

    // Listen to LoginEvent platform event
    public static void monitorLogins() {
        // Create event subscription using Apex
        EventBus.TriggerContext context = EventBus.TriggerContext.currentContext();

        List<LoginEventStream> loginEvents = (List<LoginEventStream>) Trigger.new;

        for (LoginEventStream event : loginEvents) {
            if (event.Status == 'Failed') {
                handleFailedLogin(event);
            } else if (event.Status == 'Success') {
                validateSuccessfulLogin(event);
            }
        }
    }

    private static void handleFailedLogin(LoginEventStream event) {
        // Log failed attempt
        System.debug('Failed login: ' + event.Username + 
                    ' from IP: ' + event.SourceIp);

        // Check for brute force pattern
        Integer recentFailures = countRecentFailures(event.Username);

        if (recentFailures > 5) {
            // Lock user account or send alert
            freezeUser(event.UserId);
        }
    }

    private static void validateSuccessfulLogin(LoginEventStream event) {
        // Check for impossible travel
        // (login from two distant locations in short time)

        LoginHistory lastLogin = getLastLoginLocation(event.UserId);

        if (lastLogin != null) {
            Double distanceKm = calculateDistance(
                lastLogin.CountryIso,
                event.CountryIso
            );

            Long minutesBetween = calculateMinutes(
                lastLogin.LoginTime,
                event.LoginTime
            );

            // If travel would require > 1000 km/hr, flag as suspicious
            if (distanceKm / (minutesBetween / 60.0) > 1000) {
                sendImpossibleTravelAlert(event.UserId, event.Username);
            }
        }
    }

    private static Integer countRecentFailures(String username) {
        // Count failed logins in last hour
        DateTime oneHourAgo = DateTime.now().addHours(-1);

        return [
            SELECT COUNT()
            FROM LoginHistory
            WHERE LoginTime >= :oneHourAgo
            AND Status = 'Failed'
            AND Username = :username
        ];
    }

    private static void freezeUser(Id userId) {
        User u = new User(Id = userId, IsActive = false);
        update u;

        // Send notification to security team
        sendSecurityNotification('User frozen: ' + userId);
    }

    private static LoginHistory getLastLoginLocation(Id userId) {
        List<LoginHistory> history = [
            SELECT Id, CountryIso, LoginTime
            FROM LoginHistory
            WHERE UserId = :userId
            ORDER BY LoginTime DESC
            LIMIT 2
        ];

        return history.size() > 1 ? history[1] : null;
    }

    private static Double calculateDistance(String country1, String country2) {
        // Simplified distance calculation
        // Production code should use actual coordinates
        return country1 == country2 ? 0 : 5000;
    }

    private static Long calculateMinutes(DateTime time1, DateTime time2) {
        return (time2.getTime() - time1.getTime()) / (1000 * 60);
    }

    private static void sendImpossibleTravelAlert(Id userId, String username) {

        // Send alert to security team

    private static void sendSecurityNotification(String message) {

Compliance Reports:

public class ComplianceReporter {

    // Generate access audit report
    public static void generateAccessReport(Date startDate, Date endDate) {
        List<EventLogFile> logs = [
            SELECT Id, EventType, LogDate
            FROM EventLogFile
            WHERE EventType IN ('Report', 'Dashboard', 'Document')
            AND LogDate >= :startDate
            AND LogDate <= :endDate
        ];

        Map<String, Integer> accessCounts = new Map<String, Integer>();

        for (EventLogFile log : logs) {
            String content = EventMonitoringService.getLogFileContent(log.Id);
            List<Map<String, String>> records = 
                EventMonitoringService.parseLogFile(content);

            for (Map<String, String> record : records) {
                String username = record.get('USER_NAME');
                Integer count = accessCounts.get(username);
                accessCounts.put(username, (count == null ? 1 : count + 1));
            }
        }

        // Generate report
        System.debug('Access Report: ' + accessCounts);
    }

    // Track privileged user activity
    public static void auditPrivilegedUsers() {
        // Get users with sensitive permissions
        Set<Id> privilegedUsers = getPrivilegedUsers();

        // Track their activities
        List<EventLogFile> logs = [
            SELECT Id, EventType, LogDate
            FROM EventLogFile
            WHERE EventType = 'LoginAs'
            AND LogDate = TODAY
        ];

        for (EventLogFile log : logs) {
            String content = EventMonitoringService.getLogFileContent(log.Id);
            List<Map<String, String>> records = 
                EventMonitoringService.parseLogFile(content);

            for (Map<String, String> record : records) {
                String delegatedUser = record.get('DELEGATED_USER_NAME');
                System.debug('Admin accessed as: ' + delegatedUser);
            }
        }
    }

    private static Set<Id> getPrivilegedUsers() {
        Set<Id> userIds = new Set<Id>();

        List<User> admins = [
            SELECT Id 
            FROM User 
            WHERE Profile.Name = 'System Administrator'
            AND IsActive = true
        ];

        for (User u : admins) {
            userIds.add(u.Id);
        }

        return userIds;
    }
}
