docs.title: Q: What is Pentaho Data Integration (PDI) and what are its key components?
docs.text:
A: Pentaho Data Integration, also known as Kettle, is an open-source ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) tool that enables data integration across various sources and destinations. It provides a visual development environment for designing data pipelines.

Key Components:

Spoon:

  • Definition: Graphical design interface for creating transformations and jobs
  • Purpose: Visual development environment
  • Features: Drag-and-drop interface, step configuration, preview data
  • Platform: Desktop application (Windows, Linux, macOS)

Pan:

  • Definition: Command-line tool for executing transformations
  • Usage: pan.sh -file=/path/to/transformation.ktr -level=Basic
  • Purpose: Production execution of transformations
  • Features: Headless execution, logging, parameter passing

Kitchen:

  • Definition: Command-line tool for executing jobs
  • Usage: kitchen.sh -file=/path/to/job.kjb -level=Detailed
  • Purpose: Production execution of jobs
  • Features: Scheduling integration, error handling, job orchestration

Carte:

  • Definition: Web server for remote execution
  • Purpose: Distributed processing and clustering
  • Features: REST API, load balancing, remote monitoring

Key Concepts:

Transformations (.ktr files):

  • Single-threaded execution within each step
  • Multi-threaded execution across steps
  • Data flows between steps in rowsets
  • Used for data processing and transformation

Jobs (.kjb files):

  • Sequential or conditional execution
  • Orchestrate multiple transformations
  • Control flow and error handling
  • Scheduling and workflow management

Steps vs Entries:

  • Steps: Building blocks in transformations (e.g., Table Input, Filter Rows)
  • Entries: Building blocks in jobs (e.g., Start, Transformation, Success)

Architecture:

Data Sources → [Extraction] → [Transformation] → [Loading] → Target Systems
                    ↓              ↓                ↓
                 Input Steps   Processing Steps  Output Steps

Use Cases:

Data Migration:

  • Move data between systems
  • Database upgrades
  • System consolidations
  • Legacy system decommissioning

Data Warehousing:

  • ETL processes for data warehouses
  • Dimension and fact table loading
  • Slowly changing dimensions (SCD)
  • Data mart population

Data Integration:

  • Real-time data synchronization
  • Master data management
  • API integration
  • File processing automation

Data Quality:

  • Data cleansing and standardization
  • Duplicate detection
  • Validation and error handling
  • Data profiling

Deployment Models:

  • On-Premises: Traditional server installation
  • Cloud: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud deployments
  • Hybrid: Mix of on-premises and cloud
  • Containerized: Docker and Kubernetes

Advantages:

✅ Visual development environment

✅ Wide range of supported data sources

✅ Active community and extensive documentation

✅ No per-row licensing costs

✅ Scalable for large data volumes

✅ Cross-platform compatibility

Limitations:

⚠️ Memory consumption for large datasets

⚠️ Limited real-time streaming capabilities

⚠️ Performance dependent on system resources

⚠️ Complexity increases with large projects

Best Practices:

✅ Use consistent naming conventions

✅ Document transformations and jobs

✅ Implement error handling

✅ Use parameters for flexibility

✅ Version control (Git) for .ktr and .kjb files

✅ Test thoroughly in development environment

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is the difference between a Transformation and a Job in PDI?
docs.text:
A: Transformations and Jobs are the two primary building blocks in PDI, each serving distinct purposes in the data integration process.

Transformations (.ktr):

Characteristics:

  • Execution: Parallel, multi-threaded processing
  • Data Flow: Rows flow between steps continuously
  • Purpose: Data extraction, transformation, and loading
  • Building Blocks: Steps (Input, Transform, Output, Utility)
  • Flow Type: Data flow (rowsets)

Execution Model:

[Table Input] → [Filter Rows] → [Calculator] → [Table Output]
      ↓               ↓              ↓              ↓
   (Thread 1)     (Thread 2)    (Thread 3)    (Thread 4)

Common Steps:

Input Steps:

  • Table Input (database queries)
  • Text File Input (CSV, TXT)
  • Excel Input (XLS, XLSX)
  • JSON Input
  • XML Input
  • REST Client

Transform Steps:

  • Select Values (rename, reorder columns)
  • Filter Rows (conditional filtering)
  • Calculator (calculations, functions)
  • String Operations (concatenate, replace)
  • Add Sequence (generate IDs)
  • Sort Rows (ordering data)

Output Steps:

  • Table Output (database inserts/updates)
  • Text File Output
  • Insert/Update (upsert operations)
  • Excel Output
  • JSON Output

Jobs (.kjb):

Characteristics:

  • Execution: Sequential (unless parallel specified)
  • Control Flow: Conditional execution paths
  • Purpose: Workflow orchestration
  • Building Blocks: Entries (Start, Transformations, Checks, Mail)
  • Flow Type: Control flow (success/failure)

Execution Model:

[Start] → [Check Files] → [Transformation 1] → [Success Check]
                                ↓ (Success)          ↓
                          [Transformation 2]  → [Send Email]
                                ↓ (Failure)
                           [Error Handler]

Common Entries:

Start Entries:

  • Start (entry point)

General Entries:

  • Transformation (execute .ktr)
  • Job (execute nested .kjb)
  • Shell (execute scripts)
  • SQL (run SQL scripts)
  • Mail (send notifications)

File Management:

  • Copy Files
  • Delete Files
  • File Exists
  • Wait for File

Flow Control:

  • Success (next on success)
  • Failure (next on failure)
  • Unconditional (always execute)
  • Evaluation (conditional)

Comparison:

When to Use Transformations:

  • Processing data records
  • Reading from sources
  • Transforming data
  • Writing to destinations
  • Data validation
  • Column calculations

When to Use Jobs:

  • Orchestrating multiple transformations
  • Conditional execution logic
  • File system operations
  • Email notifications
  • Error handling workflows
  • Scheduling and automation

Example Scenario:

Daily Sales ETL Process:

Job: Daily_Sales_ETL.kjb
├── [Start]
├── [Check if source file exists] (File Exists)
├── [Extract Sales Data] (Transformation)
│   └── Transformation: extract_sales.ktr
│       ├── [CSV File Input]
│       ├── [Data Validation]
│       ├── [Lookup Customer IDs]
│       └── [Table Output to Staging]
├── [Transform Sales Data] (Transformation)
│   └── Transformation: transform_sales.ktr
│       ├── [Table Input from Staging]
│       ├── [Calculate Totals]
│       ├── [Apply Business Rules]
│       └── [Table Output to DW]
├── [Success Check]
├── [Send Success Email] (on success)
└── [Send Error Email] (on failure)

Transformation Example:

<!-- Simplified .ktr structure -->
<transformation>
  <step>
    <name>CSV Input</name>
    <type>CsvInput</type>
    <filename>sales_data.csv</filename>
  </step>

  <step>
    <name>Filter Rows</name>
    <type>FilterRows</type>
    <condition>amount > 0</condition>
  </step>

  <step>
    <name>Table Output</name>
    <type>TableOutput</type>
    <connection>DataWarehouse</connection>
    <table>fact_sales</table>
  </step>

  <hop>
    <from>CSV Input</from>
    <to>Filter Rows</to>
  </hop>

  <hop>
    <from>Filter Rows</from>
    <to>Table Output</to>
  </hop>
</transformation>

Job Example:

<!-- Simplified .kjb structure -->
<job>
  <entry>
    <name>START</name>
    <type>SPECIAL</type>
    <start>Y</start>
  </entry>

  <entry>
    <name>Run Sales Extract</name>
    <type>TRANS</type>
    <filename>extract_sales.ktr</filename>
  </entry>

  <entry>
    <name>Success Email</name>
    <type>MAIL</type>
    <server>smtp.company.com</server>
    <subject>Sales ETL Completed</subject>
  </entry>

  <hop>
    <from>START</from>
    <to>Run Sales Extract</to>
  </hop>

  <hop>
    <from>Run Sales Extract</from>
    <to>Success Email</to>
    <evaluation>Y</evaluation>
  </hop>
</job>

Key Differences Summary:

Transformations:

  • ✅ Parallel execution (faster)
  • ✅ Row-based processing
  • ✅ Data transformations
  • ❌ Limited control flow
  • ❌ Cannot call other transformations directly

Jobs:

  • ✅ Control flow orchestration
  • ✅ Error handling
  • ✅ Conditional execution
  • ✅ Can call transformations and jobs
  • ❌ Sequential by default (slower)

Best Practices:

✅ Use transformations for data processing

✅ Use jobs for workflow orchestration

✅ Keep transformations focused on single tasks

✅ Use jobs for complex conditional logic

✅ Implement error handling in jobs

✅ Pass parameters from jobs to transformations

✅ Use meaningful names for both

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How does data flow work in PDI transformations?
docs.text:
A: Understanding data flow in PDI transformations is crucial for designing efficient ETL processes. PDI uses a unique parallel processing model that differs from traditional sequential ETL tools.

Data Flow Characteristics:

Parallel Processing:

  • Each step runs in its own thread
  • Multiple steps execute simultaneously
  • Data flows through rowsets (buffers)
  • Non-blocking architecture

Rowset Buffers:

  • Default buffer size: 10,000 rows
  • Configurable per transformation
  • Memory-based data transfer
  • First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue

Execution Model:

Source Step (Thread 1)
    ↓ [Rowset Buffer]
Transform Step 1 (Thread 2)
    ↓ [Rowset Buffer]
Transform Step 2 (Thread 3)
    ↓ [Rowset Buffer]
Target Step (Thread 4)

All threads execute simultaneously!

Hops (Connections):

Types of Hops:

Main Output Hop:

  • Primary data flow path
  • Black line in Spoon
  • Most common connection type

Error Handling Hop:

  • Red line in Spoon
  • Routes error rows to error handling
  • Configured in step properties

Target Steps Hop:

  • Used for specific routing
  • Multiple output paths from single step

Data Distribution:

Copy Rows to Result:

  • Passes data to next transformation in job
  • Used for transformation chaining
  • Memory-based storage

Get Rows from Result:

  • Receives data from previous transformation
  • Complements Copy Rows to Result

Example Flow:

[Table Input: Read Orders]
        ↓
[Filter Rows: Amount > 1000]
    ↓ (True)       ↓ (False)
[High Value]    [Low Value]
    ↓               ↓
[DB Output 1]   [DB Output 2]

Step Distribution:

When Multiple Copies of a Step:

[Input Step]
    ↓ (Distribute data)
    ├─→ [Step Copy 1] (25% of rows)
    ├─→ [Step Copy 2] (25% of rows)
    ├─→ [Step Copy 3] (25% of rows)
    └─→ [Step Copy 4] (25% of rows)

Distribution Methods:

  • Round Robin: Evenly distribute rows
  • Load Balanced: Based on processing time
  • Random: Random distribution

Data Flow Patterns:

Linear Flow:

[Source] → [Transform 1] → [Transform 2] → [Target]

Split Flow:

           ├→ [Branch 1] → [Target 1]
[Source] → ├→ [Branch 2] → [Target 2]
           └→ [Branch 3] → [Target 3]

Merge Flow:

[Source 1] → 
             ↓
           [Merge] → [Transform] → [Target]
             ↑
[Source 2] →

Conditional Flow:

[Source] → [Filter]
           ├→ (True) → [Process A] → [Target A]
           └→ (False) → [Process B] → [Target B]

Performance Implications:

Buffer Size Configuration:

# In transformation settings or spoon.sh/bat
KETTLE_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE=10000
KETTLE_MAX_BUFFER_LINE_SIZE=5000

Memory Usage:

  • Each rowset buffer consumes memory
  • More steps = more memory required
  • Large buffers = higher memory consumption
  • Balance between performance and resources

Blocking Steps:

Steps that Block Data Flow:

  • Sort Rows: Must read all rows before sorting
  • Group By: Must accumulate groups
  • Unique Rows: Must see all rows to find duplicates
  • Merge Join: Requires sorted input

Impact:

[Input: 1M rows] → [Sort Rows] → [Output]
                      ↑
              (Blocks until all rows read)
              (High memory usage)

Non-Blocking Alternative:

[Input: 1M rows] → [Filter Rows] → [Output]
                      ↑
              (Streams through immediately)
              (Low memory usage)

Data Flow Optimization:

Best Practices:

✅ Minimize blocking steps

✅ Use appropriate buffer sizes

✅ Filter early to reduce data volume

✅ Sort data at source when possible

✅ Monitor memory usage

✅ Use step copies for parallel processing

✅ Avoid unnecessary transformations

Example - Optimized Flow:

[Table Input: SELECT with WHERE]  ← Filter at source
        ↓
[Select Values: Remove unneeded columns]  ← Reduce data size
        ↓
[Calculator: Only necessary calculations]
        ↓
[Table Output]

Example - Inefficient Flow:

[Table Input: SELECT *]  ← Retrieves all columns
        ↓
[Calculator: Multiple complex calculations]
        ↓
[Sort Rows: Full dataset sort]  ← Blocking, memory intensive
        ↓
[Filter Rows]  ← Should be earlier
        ↓
[Select Values]  ← Too late
        ↓
[Table Output]

Monitoring Data Flow:

Preview Feature:

  • Right-click step → Preview
  • Shows sample data at that point
  • Useful for debugging

Logging:

  • Enable row-level logging
  • Monitor row count per step
  • Check for bottlenecks

Metrics Tab:

  • View step execution time
  • Check rows read/written
  • Identify slow steps

Common Issues:

Slow Performance:

  • Too many blocking steps
  • Large buffer sizes
  • Insufficient memory
  • Complex transformations

Memory Errors:

  • Buffer size too large
  • Too many concurrent steps
  • Blocking steps with large datasets
  • Insufficient heap size

Data Loss:

  • Missing error handling hops
  • Incorrect filtering
  • Buffer overflow (rare)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What are the most commonly used transformation steps in PDI?
docs.text:
A: PDI provides hundreds of steps for various data integration tasks. Understanding the most common steps and their use cases is essential for effective ETL development.

Input Steps:

Table Input:

-- Most commonly used step for database queries
SELECT 
    customer_id,
    customer_name,
    email,
    registration_date
FROM customers
WHERE active = 'Y'
AND registration_date >= ?  -- Parameter placeholder

Use Cases:

  • Extract data from databases
  • Parameterized queries
  • Large dataset extraction
  • Incremental loads

Configuration:

  • Connection: Database connection
  • SQL: Query text
  • Enable lazy conversion: Better performance
  • Replace variables in script: Use ${VARIABLE}

Text File Input:

Supported Formats:

  • CSV (Comma-Separated Values)
  • TSV (Tab-Separated Values)
  • Fixed Width
  • Custom delimiters

Configuration:

Filename: /data/sales_*.csv  (wildcard support)
Delimiter: ,
Enclosure: "
Header: Y
Encoding: UTF-8
Format: Unix/Windows/Mixed

Best Practices:

✅ Use wildcards for multiple files

✅ Specify correct encoding

✅ Define data types explicitly

✅ Handle headers appropriately

✅ Use Get Fields to auto-detect structure

Excel Input:

Features:

  • Read multiple sheets
  • Skip rows
  • Start from specific cell
  • Password-protected files

Configuration:

File: sales_report.xlsx
Sheet: Sheet1
Start Row: 2 (skip header)
Start Column: A
Stop on empty row: Y
Fields: Auto-detect or manual

JSON Input:

Configuration:

Source: File/Field/URL
Path: JSONPath expression
$.store.books[*]  (all books in store)

XML Input:

Features:

  • XPath expressions
  • Loop over nodes
  • Extract attributes
  • Namespace support

Transform Steps:

Select Values:

Primary Functions:

  • Select & Rename: Choose and rename fields
  • Remove: Delete unwanted fields
  • Change Metadata: Modify data types, lengths, precision

Configuration:

Select & Rename:
  Field: old_name → new_name
  Type: String → Integer
  Length: 255 → 10
  Format: MM/dd/yyyy

Remove:
  - temporary_field
  - debug_column

Use Cases:

  • Clean up field names
  • Remove unnecessary columns
  • Change data types
  • Reorder fields

Filter Rows:

Conditions:

Simple Condition:
  Field: amount
  Condition: >
  Value: 1000

Complex Condition:
  (amount > 1000 AND status = 'ACTIVE')
  OR
  (priority = 'HIGH')

Configuration:

  • Send 'true' data to: Next step (matching condition)
  • Send 'false' data to: Alternative path
  • Condition: JavaScript or simple

Calculator:

Functions:

Mathematical:

  • A + B (Addition)
  • A - B (Subtraction)
  • A * B (Multiplication)
  • A / B (Division)
  • SQRT(A), ABS(A), ROUND(A,B)

Date Functions:

  • Add days to date
  • Year/Month/Day of date
  • Date difference
  • Date working days

String Functions:

  • Concatenate (A + B)
  • Length of string
  • Trim spaces

Example:

Field A: unit_price (100)
Field B: quantity (5)
Field C: tax_rate (0.08)

Calculation:
total = unit_price * quantity
tax = total * tax_rate
grand_total = total + tax

Result:
total = 500
tax = 40
grand_total = 540

String Operations:

Functions:

  • Lower case
  • Upper case
  • Capitalize
  • Trim (left/right/both)
  • Padding
  • Remove digits
  • Remove special characters

Configuration:

In Stream Field: customer_name
Operation: Trim (both)
→ "  John Doe  " becomes "John Doe"

In Stream Field: email
Operation: Lower case
→ "USER@EMAIL.COM" becomes "user@email.com"

Add Sequence:

Valuename: row_id
Start value: 1
Increment by: 1
Max value: 999999999

Use Cases:

  • Generate surrogate keys
  • Add row numbers
  • Create unique identifiers

Sort Rows:

Configuration:

Fields to sort:
  1. customer_id (Ascending)
  2. order_date (Descending)
  3. amount (Descending)

Options:
- Only pass unique rows: N
- Sort size (rows in memory): 5000
- Free memory threshold %: 0

⚠️ Warning: Blocking step - reads all rows before sorting

Alternatives:

  • Sort at database level (ORDER BY in SQL)
  • Use pre-sorted data when possible

Lookup Steps:

Database Lookup:

-- Lookup customer details
SELECT 
    customer_name,
    customer_type,
    credit_limit
FROM dim_customer
WHERE customer_id = ?  -- Lookup key

Configuration:

  • Connection: Target database
  • Schema/Table: dim_customer
  • Lookup field: customer_id
  • Compare field: customer_id from stream
  • Return fields: customer_name, type, limit

Stream Lookup:

Process:

  1. Load lookup data into memory
  2. Create hash table
  3. Lookup rows from main stream

Configuration:

  • Lookup step: Source of lookup data
  • Keys: Fields to match
  • Values: Fields to retrieve

Memory Consideration:

⚠️ Entire lookup table loaded into memory

✅ Best for small to medium lookup tables (<100K rows)

❌ Avoid for large lookup tables (>1M rows)

Output Steps:

Table Output:

Configuration:

Connection: Target database
Target schema: public
Target table: fact_sales
Commit size: 1000  (rows per commit)
Use batch: Y
Truncate table: N
Specify database fields: Y

Options:

  • Truncate: Delete all data before insert
  • Use batch: Batch inserts for performance
  • Ignore errors: Continue on error
  • Return auto-generated key: Get identity values

Insert/Update:

Upsert Logic:

Lookup field: customer_id
Update field: customer_id

If exists: UPDATE
  - customer_name
  - email
  - last_updated

If not exists: INSERT
  - All fields

Best Practices:

✅ Use appropriate lookup keys

✅ Define update fields explicitly

✅ Set proper commit size

✅ Test with small datasets first

Text File Output:

Configuration:

Filename: /output/sales_${date}.csv
Extension: csv
Create parent folder: Y
Append: N
Split every X rows: 0 (no split)
Fields:
  - Separator: ,
  - Enclosure: "
  - Force enclosure: N
  - Header: Y
  - Footer: N

Best Practices:

✅ Use date/time in filename

✅ Create parent folders automatically

✅ Handle special characters with enclosure

✅ Include headers for readability

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How do you implement Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD) in PDI?
docs.text:
A: Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD) are a data warehousing technique for tracking changes in dimension tables over time. PDI provides dedicated steps for implementing SCD Types 1, 2, and 3.

SCD Types Overview:

Type 1 - Overwrite:

  • Simply update the record
  • No history maintained
  • Simplest implementation

Type 2 - Add New Row:

  • Add new record for changes
  • Keep historical records
  • Use effective dates and flags

Type 3 - Add New Column:

  • Store previous value in same row
  • Limited history (current + one previous)
  • Rarely used

SCD Type 1 Implementation:

Using Insert/Update Step:

[Source Data]
      ↓
[Lookup Dimension Values]
      ↓
[Filter Changed Records]
      ↓
[Insert/Update]
    (Overwrite existing records)

Configuration:

Insert/Update Step:
- Table: dim_customer
- Lookup Keys: customer_id
- Update fields:
  * customer_name
  * email
  * phone
  * last_updated_date

Example:

Before:
customer_id | name      | email
1          | John Doe  | john@old.com

After Update:
customer_id | name      | email
1          | John Doe  | john@new.com  ← Email updated

SCD Type 2 Implementation:

Using Dimension Lookup/Update Step:

Transformation Structure:

[Source: Customer Data]
        ↓
[Dimension Lookup/Update]
  - Check for changes
  - Insert new version
  - Expire old version
        ↓
[Table Output]

Dimension Lookup/Update Configuration:

Keys Tab:

Dimension field: customer_id
Field in stream: customer_id

Fields Tab:

Dimension field | Type    | Stream field
customer_name   | Update  | name
email          | Update  | email
phone          | Update  | phone
address        | Update  | address

Technical Key:

Field: customer_key
Auto-increment: Checked
Version field: version

Dates:

Date range start: valid_from
Date range end: valid_to

Implementation:

-- Before change:
customer_key | customer_id | name     | email        | valid_from | valid_to   | current
1           | 100         | John Doe | john@old.com | 2023-01-01 | 9999-12-31 | Y

-- After change (email updated):
customer_key | customer_id | name     | email        | valid_from | valid_to   | current
1           | 100         | John Doe | john@old.com | 2023-01-01 | 2024-12-31 | N  ← Expired
2           | 100         | John Doe | john@new.com | 2025-01-01 | 9999-12-31 | Y  ← New version

Complete SCD Type 2 Transformation:

[Table Input: Source System]
SELECT 
  customer_id,
  customer_name,
  email,
  phone,
  address
FROM source_customers
        ↓
[Data Validation]
  - Check for nulls
  - Validate email format
  - Trim spaces
        ↓
[Dimension Lookup/Update]
  - Compare with existing dimension
  - Detect changes
  - Insert new versions
  - Expire old versions
        ↓
[Log Changes] (Optional)
  - Track what changed
  - Audit logging
        ↓
[Success]

SCD Type 2 with Multiple Dimensions:

[Fact Table Load]
        ↓
[Lookup: Customer Dimension]
  → Get current customer_key
        ↓
[Lookup: Product Dimension]
  → Get current product_key
        ↓
[Lookup: Date Dimension]
  → Get date_key
        ↓
[Table Output: Fact Table]
  - fact_key
  - customer_key  ← SCD Type 2 key
  - product_key   ← SCD Type 2 key
  - date_key
  - amount
  - quantity

Advanced SCD Patterns:

Hybrid Approach:

[Source Data]
        ↓
[Compare with Dimension]
        ↓
    [Filter]
        ├─→ No Change → [Skip]
        ├─→ Type 1 Change → [Update existing]
        └─→ Type 2 Change → [Insert new version]

Type 1 vs Type 2 Decision:

Changes to track (Type 2):
- Address changes
- Status changes
- Pricing tier changes

Corrections (Type 1):
- Spelling errors
- Phone number updates
- Email updates

Implementation Code:

-- Dimension table structure
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
    customer_key BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,  -- Surrogate key
    customer_id VARCHAR(50),          -- Business key
    customer_name VARCHAR(100),
    email VARCHAR(100),
    phone VARCHAR(20),
    address VARCHAR(200),
    city VARCHAR(50),
    state VARCHAR(2),
    zip VARCHAR(10),
    valid_from DATE,
    valid_to DATE,
    is_current CHAR(1),              -- Y/N
    version INTEGER,
    created_date TIMESTAMP,
    updated_date TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE INDEX idx_customer_id ON dim_customer(customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_current ON dim_customer(is_current);

Performance Optimization:

Lookup Performance:

[Source Data]
        ↓
[Sort by customer_id]  ← Pre-sort if possible
        ↓
[Stream Lookup]  ← Use for large dimensions
   (Pre-load dimension into memory)
        ↓
[Filter Changes]
        ↓
[Insert New/Update Existing]

Batch Processing:

Instead of:
- Process 1 record at a time
- Lookup each record individually

Use:
- Batch processing (10,000+ records)
- Bulk lookups
- Bulk inserts/updates

Best Practices:

✅ Use surrogate keys (auto-increment)

✅ Index business keys for fast lookups

✅ Use meaningful date ranges

✅ Implement current record flag

✅ Version dimensions for tracking

✅ Test with historical data

✅ Document change rules

✅ Handle null values appropriately

✅ Consider late-arriving dimensions

Error Handling:

[Dimension Lookup/Update]
        ↓
     [Check for Errors]
        ├─→ Success → [Log Success]
        └─→ Error → [Error Handler]
                    ├─→ [Log Error]
                    └─→ [Move to Error Table]

Common Issues:

Memory Issues:

❌ Loading large dimension tables into memory

✅ Use database lookups for large tables

✅ Limit lookup fields to necessary columns

Performance:

❌ Individual record updates

✅ Batch updates

✅ Use appropriate commit sizes

Data Quality:

❌ Null business keys

❌ Duplicate business keys

✅ Validate data before dimension update

✅ Implement data quality rules

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How do you create and schedule PDI jobs?
docs.text:
A: PDI Jobs orchestrate workflows, execute transformations, and implement error handling. Scheduling can be done through operating system schedulers or enterprise schedulers.

Job Components:

Start Entry:

[START]  ← Entry point (required)
  ↓
[First Job Entry]

Configuration:

  • Every job must have exactly one START entry
  • No configuration needed
  • Green flag icon
  • Beginning of control flow

Transformation Entry:

Configuration:

Transformation:
- Filename: /path/to/transformation.ktr
- Run configuration: Local
- Parameters:
  * INPUT_DATE = ${TODAY}
  * BATCH_SIZE = 10000
- Log level: Basic
- Clear log before execution: Y

Pass Parameters:

Job Parameters → Transformation
${JOB_START_DATE} → ${TRANS_DATE}
${SOURCE_FILE} → ${INPUT_FILE}

Execute Results:

Execution Metrics:
- Rows read: 50,000
- Rows written: 49,875
- Rows updated: 125
- Errors: 0
- Execution time: 45 seconds

Job Entry:

Nested Jobs:

[Parent Job]
    ↓
[Sub-Job 1] → [Sub-Job 2] → [Sub-Job 3]

Use Cases:

  • Modular design
  • Reusable workflows
  • Complex dependencies
  • Error isolation

SQL Entry:

Execute SQL Script:

-- Pre-processing
TRUNCATE TABLE staging_orders;

-- Create indexes
CREATE INDEX idx_order_date 
ON staging_orders(order_date);

-- Maintenance
VACUUM ANALYZE staging_orders;

-- Post-processing
UPDATE control_table 
SET last_run_date = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE job_name = 'sales_etl';

Configuration:

Connection: Database connection
SQL script:
  - From file
  - Inline SQL
  - Variable substitution: ${SQL_FILE}
Execute for each row: N (usually)
Send SQL as single statement: Y

Shell Entry:

Execute Scripts:

#!/bin/bash
# Archive processed files
DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d)
mkdir -p /archive/$DATE
mv /input/*.csv /archive/$DATE/

# Cleanup old files
find /archive -mtime +30 -delete

# Check disk space
df -h / | awk 'NR==2 {if ($5+0 > 90) exit 1}'

Configuration:

Script:
- File: /scripts/archive_files.sh
- Working directory: /data
- Log file: /logs/shell_${date}.log
- Insert script: Y (inline script)
- Execute for each row: N

Mail Entry:

Send Notifications:

Configuration:
- Destination:
  * To: team@company.com
  * CC: manager@company.com
  * BCC: audit@company.com

- Server:
  * SMTP server: smtp.company.com
  * Port: 587
  * Authentication: Y
  * Use SSL/TLS: Y

- Message:
  * Subject: ${JOB_NAME} - ${STATUS}
  * Body:
    Job: ${JOB_NAME}
    Status: ${STATUS}
    Start time: ${START_TIME}
    End time: ${END_TIME}
    Rows processed: ${ROWS_PROCESSED}

- Attachments:
  * Log file
  * Error report

Wait For Entry:

Wait for File:

Configuration:
- Filename: /input/sales_${TODAY}.csv
- Maximum timeout: 3600 seconds (1 hour)
- Check cycle time: 60 seconds
- Success when file exists: Y
- Add filename to result: Y

File Operations:

Copy Files:

Configuration:
- Source:
  * Directory: /input
  * Wildcard: sales_*.csv
- Destination:
  * Directory: /processed/${TODAY}
  * Create folder: Y
- Options:
  * Overwrite files: N
  * Remove source files: Y
  * Add result filenames: Y

Delete Files:

Configuration:
- File/Folder: /temp/*.tmp
- Include subfolders: Y
- Success condition:
  * Success when all deleted
  * Success when at least X deleted

Check Files Exist:

Configuration:
- Files to check:
  1. /input/customers.csv
  2. /input/orders.csv
  3. /input/products.csv
- Condition:
  * All files exist
  * At least one exists
  * Exactly X files exist

Job Flow Control:

Success/Failure Hops:

[Transformation]
    ↓ (Success - Green)
[Send Success Email]
    ↓ (Failure - Red)
[Send Error Email]
    ↓ (Unconditional - Black)
[Cleanup Files]

Evaluation:

[Check Records Processed]
  ↓ (Evaluation)
IF ${RECORDS_PROCESSED} > 0
  THEN → [Send Summary Email]
  ELSE → [Send No Data Email]

Scheduling Methods:

1. Cron (Linux/Unix):

# Edit crontab
crontab -e

# Daily at 2:00 AM
0 2 * * * /opt/pentaho/kitchen.sh \
  -file=/etl/jobs/daily_sales_etl.kjb \
  -level=Basic \
  -param:RUN_DATE=$(date +\%Y-\%m-\%d) \
  >> /logs/sales_etl_$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).log 2>&1

# Every 15 minutes
*/15 * * * * /opt/pentaho/kitchen.sh \
  -file=/etl/jobs/incremental_sync.kjb

# Monday-Friday at 6:00 PM
0 18 * * 1-5 /opt/pentaho/kitchen.sh \
  -file=/etl/jobs/weekly_reports.kjb

2. Windows Task Scheduler:

REM Create batch file: run_etl.bat
@echo off
SET PENTAHO_HOME=C:\pentaho
SET JOB_FILE=%PENTAHO_HOME%\jobs\daily_etl.kjb
SET LOG_DIR=C:\logs
SET RUN_DATE=%date:~-4%-%date:~-10,2%-%date:~-7,2%

cd %PENTAHO_HOME%
call kitchen.bat ^
  -file=%JOB_FILE% ^
  -level=Detailed ^
  -param:RUN_DATE=%RUN_DATE% ^
  >> %LOG_DIR%\etl_%RUN_DATE%.log 2>&1

Schedule Task:

1. Open Task Scheduler
2. Create Basic Task
3. Name: Daily Sales ETL
4. Trigger: Daily at 2:00 AM
5. Action: Start a program
   - Program: C:\etl\run_etl.bat
6. Conditions: Start only if computer is on AC power
7. Settings: Run task as soon as possible if missed

3. Enterprise Schedulers:

Control-M Example:

<JOB NAME="DAILY_SALES_ETL"
     APPLICATION="ETL"
     SUB_APPLICATION="SALES">
  <ON_DO STMT="OS_COMMAND" 
          CMDLINE="/opt/pentaho/kitchen.sh -file=/etl/jobs/daily_sales.kjb"
          USER="etl_user"/>
  <QUANTITATIVE NAME="RECORDS_PROCESSED" 
                OPER="GE" 
                VALUE="1"/>
  <ON STMT="SUCCESS" 
      CODE="OK"/>
  <ON STMT="FAILURE" 
      CODE="NOTOK"/>
</JOB>

Autosys Example:

insert_job: sales_etl
job_type: c
command: /opt/pentaho/kitchen.sh -file=/etl/jobs/daily_sales.kjb
machine: etl-server
owner: etl_user
permission: gx,wx
date_conditions: 1
days_of_week: mo,tu,we,th,fr
start_times: "02:00"
std_out_file: /logs/sales_etl_${date}.log
std_err_file: /logs/sales_etl_${date}.err
alarm_if_fail: 1

Job Monitoring:

Kitchen Execution:

# Execute job with detailed logging
/opt/pentaho/kitchen.sh \
  -file=/etl/jobs/daily_etl.kjb \
  -level=Detailed \
  -param:START_DATE=2025-01-01 \
  -param:END_DATE=2025-01-31 \
  -logfile=/logs/etl_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).log

Return Codes:

0 = Success
1 = Errors occurred
2 = Stopped by user
7 = Unexpected error
9 = Unable to load job

Check Return Code:

#!/bin/bash
/opt/pentaho/kitchen.sh -file=/etl/jobs/daily_etl.kjb
RESULT=$?

if [ $RESULT -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Job completed successfully"
    exit 0
else
    echo "Job failed with code $RESULT"
    # Send alert
    mail -s "ETL Job Failed" admin@company.com < /logs/error.log
    exit 1
fi

Best Practices:

✅ Use meaningful job names

✅ Implement comprehensive error handling

✅ Send notifications for failures

✅ Log execution details

✅ Pass parameters from scheduler

✅ Set appropriate timeouts

✅ Clean up temporary files

✅ Monitor job execution times

✅ Implement retry logic

✅ Document scheduling dependencies

Error Handling Pattern:

[START]
    ↓
[Check Prerequisites]
    ↓ (Success)
[Main Transformation]
    ↓ (Success)
[Validation]
    ↓ (Success)
[Cleanup]
    ↓
[Success Email]

Any Failure:
    ↓
[Error Handler]
    ↓
[Log Error Details]
    ↓
[Send Error Notification]
    ↓
[Rollback Changes]
    ↓
[END]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How do you configure and optimize database connections in PDI?
docs.text:
A: Database connections are fundamental to PDI's ETL capabilities. Proper configuration and optimization ensure reliable, performant data integration.

Database Connection Setup:

Connection Types:

Generic Database Connection:

Connection Name: MySQL_Production
Connection Type: MySQL
Access: Native (JDBC)
Host: db-server.company.com
Database: sales_db
Port: 3306
Username: etl_user
Password: ********  (encrypted)

JDBC Connection:

Connection Name: Oracle_DW
Connection Type: Oracle
Access: JDBC
Database Name: ORCL
Host Name: oracle-server.company.com
Port: 1521
Username: dwh_user
Password: ********

Supported Databases:

Relational Databases:

  • MySQL/MariaDB
  • PostgreSQL
  • Oracle
  • Microsoft SQL Server
  • IBM DB2
  • Teradata
  • SAP HANA

Data Warehouses:

  • Amazon Redshift
  • Google BigQuery
  • Snowflake
  • Azure Synapse

NoSQL:

  • MongoDB
  • Cassandra
  • HBase

Connection Parameters:

MySQL Optimization:

Options:
  useSSL=true
  rewriteBatchedStatements=true  ← Improves batch insert performance
  useServerPrepStmts=false
  useCompression=true
  connectTimeout=30000
  socketTimeout=60000

PostgreSQL Optimization:

Options:
  ssl=true
  sslmode=require
  prepareThreshold=0  ← Use server-side prepared statements
  reWriteBatchedInserts=true  ← Batch optimization
  tcpKeepAlive=true
  loginTimeout=30

Oracle Optimization:

Options:
  defaultBatchValue=1000
  useFetchSizeWithLongColumn=true
  processEscapes=false

SQL Server Optimization:

Options:
  encrypt=true
  trustServerCertificate=false
  sendStringParametersAsUnicode=false
  selectMethod=cursor  ← For large result sets
  useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true  ← Fast bulk inserts

Connection Pooling:

Configuration:

Pool Parameters:
- Initial pool size: 1
- Maximum pool size: 10
- Maximum idle connections: 5
- Maximum wait time: 30000ms
- Test connections: On borrow
- Test query: SELECT 1

Benefits:

✅ Reuse connections across transformations

✅ Reduce connection overhead

✅ Better resource management

✅ Improved performance

Custom Connection Pool:

Connection Pool Type: HikariCP
Maximum Pool Size: 20
Minimum Idle: 5
Connection Timeout: 30000
Idle Timeout: 600000
Max Lifetime: 1800000

Database Performance Optimization:

1. Efficient Queries:

❌ Poor Performance:

-- Retrieving all columns
SELECT * FROM orders;

-- No filtering
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM orders;

-- No indexes used
SELECT order_id
FROM orders
WHERE UPPER(customer_name) = 'JOHN DOE';

✅ Optimized:

-- Select only needed columns
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, order_date
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= ? 
  AND order_date < ?
  AND status = 'COMPLETED';

-- Use indexes
CREATE INDEX idx_order_date ON orders(order_date);
CREATE INDEX idx_status ON orders(status);

-- Pushdown filtering
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date = CURRENT_DATE  -- Filter at source
  AND amount > 1000;

2. Batch Operations:

Table Output Configuration:

Commit size: 10000  ← Rows per commit
Use batch: Yes  ← Enable batch inserts
Truncate table: No
Specify database fields: Yes

Performance Impact:
- Without batch: 1000 rows/sec
- With batch: 50000 rows/sec (50x faster)

3. Bulk Loading:

PostgreSQL COPY:

-- Generate CSV file
[Table Input] → [Text File Output: /tmp/data.csv]

-- Bulk load
COPY target_table
FROM '/tmp/data.csv'
WITH (FORMAT CSV, HEADER true, DELIMITER ',');

MySQL LOAD DATA:

LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/tmp/data.csv'
INTO TABLE target_table
FIELDS TERMINATED BY ','
ENCLOSED BY '"'
LINES TERMINATED BY '\n'
IGNORE 1 LINES;

4. Partitioning:

Read Partitioned Data:

-- Partition 1
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' 
  AND order_date < '2024-02-01';

-- Partition 2
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-02-01' 
  AND order_date < '2024-03-01';

-- Process in parallel
[Table Input 1] → [Process 1]
[Table Input 2] → [Process 2]
[Table Input 3] → [Process 3]

Database-Specific Optimizations:

MySQL:

-- Disable indexes during bulk load
ALTER TABLE target_table DISABLE KEYS;

-- Bulk insert
INSERT INTO target_table VALUES (...);

-- Re-enable indexes
ALTER TABLE target_table ENABLE KEYS;

-- Optimize table
OPTIMIZE TABLE target_table;

PostgreSQL:

-- Disable triggers
ALTER TABLE target_table DISABLE TRIGGER ALL;

-- Bulk load
COPY target_table FROM '/tmp/data.csv';

-- Enable triggers
ALTER TABLE target_table ENABLE TRIGGER ALL;

-- Analyze table
ANALYZE target_table;

Oracle:

-- Disable constraints
ALTER TABLE target_table DISABLE CONSTRAINT fk_constraint;

-- Direct path insert
INSERT /*+ APPEND */ INTO target_table
SELECT * FROM staging_table;

-- Enable constraints
ALTER TABLE target_table ENABLE CONSTRAINT fk_constraint;

-- Gather statistics
EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS('SCHEMA', 'TARGET_TABLE');

Connection Error Handling:

Retry Logic:

[Table Input]
    ↓
[Error Handler]
  IF connection fails:
    RETRY 3 times
    WAIT 30 seconds between retries
    LOG each attempt
  IF all retries fail:
    SEND alert
    EXIT with error

Connection Validation:

-- Test query
SELECT 1 FROM dual;  -- Oracle
SELECT 1;  -- MySQL, PostgreSQL

-- Connection test in job
[Start]
    ↓
[SQL: Test Connection]
    ↓ (Success)
[Main Processing]
    ↓ (Failure)
[Send Connection Error Email]

Secure Connections:

SSL/TLS Configuration:

MySQL SSL:
  useSSL=true
  requireSSL=true
  verifyServerCertificate=true
  trustCertificateKeyStoreUrl=file:///path/to/truststore
  trustCertificateKeyStorePassword=******

PostgreSQL SSL:
  ssl=true
  sslmode=verify-full
  sslrootcert=/path/to/root.crt
  sslcert=/path/to/client.crt
  sslkey=/path/to/client.key

Credentials Management:

Environment Variables:

# Set in shell
export DB_USERNAME=etl_user
export DB_PASSWORD=secure_password

# Use in transformation
${DB_USERNAME}
${DB_PASSWORD}

Encrypted Passwords:

# Encrypt password
encr.sh -kettle password_to_encrypt

# Use encrypted value in connection
Password: Encrypted 2be98afc86aa7f2e4cb79ce10ca97bcce

Best Practices:

✅ Use connection pooling for high-volume processes

✅ Test connections before processing

✅ Implement retry logic

✅ Use SSL/TLS for sensitive data

✅ Encrypt passwords

✅ Optimize commit sizes

✅ Use batch operations

✅ Create appropriate indexes

✅ Monitor connection usage

✅ Close connections properly

✅ Use database-specific optimizations

✅ Document connection parameters

Performance Monitoring:

-- Check active connections (PostgreSQL)
SELECT 
    datname,
    usename,
    client_addr,
    state,
    query_start,
    query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'your_database'
ORDER BY query_start;

-- Check table size
SELECT 
    schemaname,
    tablename,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(schemaname||'.'||tablename)) AS size
FROM pg_tables
WHERE schemaname = 'public'
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(schemaname||'.'||tablename) DESC;

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What are the best practices for optimizing PDI transformation performance?
docs.text:
A: Performance optimization in PDI involves understanding data flow, memory management, database operations, and transformation design patterns.

Performance Bottlenecks:

Common Issues:

  • Blocking steps (Sort, Group By)
  • Large memory consumption
  • Slow database operations
  • Inefficient transformations
  • Network latency
  • Disk I/O limitations

1. Data Volume Reduction:

Filter Early:

❌ Bad:
[Table Input: SELECT *]
    ↓ (1M rows)
[Multiple Transformations]
    ↓ (1M rows)
[Filter Rows: status = 'ACTIVE']
    ↓ (100K rows)
[Output]

✅ Good:
[Table Input: SELECT * WHERE status = 'ACTIVE']
    ↓ (100K rows - filtered at source)
[Transformations]
    ↓
[Output]

Select Only Needed Columns:

❌ Bad:
SELECT * FROM orders;  -- 50 columns

✅ Good:
SELECT 
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    order_date,
    amount,
    status
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - 7;  -- 5 columns, recent data only

2. Memory Optimization:

Increase Heap Size:

# spoon.sh (Linux/Mac)
PENTAHO_DI_JAVA_OPTIONS="-Xms2048m -Xmx8192m -XX:MaxPermSize=512m"

# spoon.bat (Windows)
set PENTAHO_DI_JAVA_OPTIONS=-Xms2048m -Xmx8192m

Adjust Buffer Sizes:

Transformation Settings → Miscellaneous:
- Number of rows in rowset: 10000 (default)
- Increase for: Better throughput, more memory
- Decrease for: Lower memory usage, slower throughput

Recommended values:
- Small data (<100K rows): 5000
- Medium data (100K-1M rows): 10000
- Large data (>1M rows): 20000

Use SOQL For Loops:

❌ Bad (High Memory):
[Table Input]
    ↓ (Load 10M rows into memory)
[Process All Rows]

✅ Good (Memory Efficient):
For each batch of 200 rows:
    [Process Batch]
    [Free Memory]

3. Database Optimization:

Connection Pooling:

Connection Settings:
- Use connection pooling: Yes
- Initial pool size: 5
- Maximum pool size: 20
- Pool prepared statements: Yes
- Max open prepared statements: 100

Batch Processing:

Table Output Settings:
- Commit size: 10000
- Use batch: Yes
- Truncate table: No (unless needed)

Performance:
- Without batch: 1,000 rows/sec
- With batch (1000): 20,000 rows/sec
- With batch (10000): 50,000 rows/sec

Parallel Processing:

[Source]
    ↓
[Step with 4 copies]
  ├─→ Copy 1 (25% of data)
  ├─→ Copy 2 (25% of data)
  ├─→ Copy 3 (25% of data)
  └─→ Copy 4 (25% of data)
    ↓
[Output]

Configure: Right-click step → Change number of copies

4. Avoid Blocking Steps:

Blocking Steps:

  • Sort Rows
  • Group By
  • Unique Rows
  • Merge Join
  • Memory Group By

Alternatives:

❌ Blocking:
[Table Input]
    ↓ (1M rows)
[Sort Rows]  ← Blocks until all rows read
    ↓
[Output]

✅ Non-Blocking:
[Table Input: ORDER BY in SQL]
    ↓ (Pre-sorted)
[Output]

5. Lookup Optimization:

Database Lookup:

❌ Slow:
- No index on lookup field
- Lookup in loop
- Individual lookups per row

✅ Fast:
- Indexed lookup fields
- Cached lookups (if small table)
- Batch lookups where possible

CREATE INDEX idx_customer_id ON customers(customer_id);

Stream Lookup:

Use when:
✅ Lookup table < 100,000 rows
✅ Memory available
✅ Frequent lookups

Avoid when:
❌ Lookup table > 1M rows
❌ Limited memory
❌ Infrequent lookups

Database Join:

-- Instead of lookup in PDI, join at database level
SELECT 
    o.order_id,
    o.amount,
    c.customer_name,
    c.email
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - 7;

6. Clustering and Load Balancing:

Carte Server Setup:

<!-- carte-config-master.xml -->
<slave_config>
  <masters>
    <slaveserver>
      <name>master</name>
      <hostname>master-server</hostname>
      <port>8080</port>
      <username>cluster</username>
      <password>password</password>
      <master>Y</master>
    </slaveserver>
  </masters>

  <slaveserver>
    <name>slave1</name>
    <hostname>slave-server-1</hostname>
    <port>8081</port>
    <username>cluster</username>
    <password>password</password>
    <master>N</master>
  </slaveserver>

  <slaveserver>
    <name>slave2</name>
    <hostname>slave-server-2</hostname>
    <port>8081</port>
    <username>cluster</username>
    <password>password</password>
    <master>N</master>
  </slaveserver>
</slave_config>

Clustered Execution:

[Source] (Master)
    ↓
Distribute to Slaves:
├─→ [Slave 1: Process 33% of data]
├─→ [Slave 2: Process 33% of data]
└─→ [Slave 3: Process 34% of data]
    ↓
[Merge Results] (Master)
    ↓
[Output]

7. Performance Monitoring:

Metrics to Track:

Transformation Metrics:
- Execution time
- Rows read per second
- Rows written per second
- Memory usage
- CPU usage
- Database connections

Step-Level Metrics:
- Input rows
- Output rows
- Errors
- Buffer usage
- Execution time

Enable Logging:

Transformation Settings → Logging:
- Log level: Detailed
- Log connection: Database connection
- Log table: trans_log
- Log batch ID: Yes
- Log field: Yes
- Log timeout: 300 seconds

8. File I/O Optimization:

Text File Input:

Configuration:
- Buffer size: 50000 (default)
- Encoding: UTF-8
- Use NIO: Yes (faster for large files)
- Lazy conversion: Yes
- Run in parallel: Yes (if multiple files)

Compression:

Text File Input:
- Compression: GZIP
- Benefit: Reduce network transfer time
- Trade-off: CPU overhead for decompression

When to use:
✅ Remote file access
✅ Network bandwidth limited
✅ Large files

9. Transformation Design:

Modular Design:

❌ Monolithic:
[One huge transformation with 50+ steps]

✅ Modular:
[Job]
├─→ [Extract Transformation]
├─→ [Transform Transformation]
└─→ [Load Transformation]

Benefits:
- Easier to maintain
- Better error isolation
- Reusable components
- Parallel execution

Minimize Hops:

❌ Excessive Hops:
[Input] → [Step 1] → [Step 2] → [Step 3] → [Step 4] → [Output]
(Each hop adds overhead)

✅ Combined Operations:
[Input] → [Combined Transformation] → [Output]
(Where possible, combine operations)

10. Best Practices Summary:

Always Do:

✅ Filter data at the source

✅ Select only needed columns

✅ Use appropriate indexes

✅ Enable batch processing

✅ Use connection pooling

✅ Monitor performance metrics

✅ Test with production-sized data

✅ Profile transformations

✅ Use parallel processing

✅ Implement caching strategically

Never Do:

❌ SOQL in loops

❌ Process all data when subset needed

❌ Use blocking steps unnecessarily

❌ Ignore memory limits

❌ Skip performance testing

❌ Load entire large tables into memory

❌ Use single-threaded when parallel possible

Performance Testing:

Test Scenarios:
1. Small dataset (1K rows): Baseline
2. Medium dataset (100K rows): Normal load
3. Large dataset (1M+ rows): Stress test
4. Multiple concurrent executions: Load test

Measure:
- Execution time
- Memory usage
- CPU usage
- Database load
- Error rates

docs.title: Q: What are common PDI errors and how do you troubleshoot them?
docs.text:
A: Effective troubleshooting in PDI requires understanding error patterns, logging mechanisms, and systematic debugging approaches.

Common Errors:

1. Out of Memory Errors:

Error Message:

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded

Causes:

  • Insufficient heap size
  • Blocking steps with large datasets
  • Memory leaks
  • Too many step copies

Solutions:

# Increase heap size
# In spoon.sh or spoon.bat
PENTAHO_DI_JAVA_OPTIONS="-Xms4096m -Xmx8192m -XX:MaxPermSize=512m"

# Monitor memory usage
jvisualvm  # Java VisualVM tool

Transformation Changes:

- Reduce rowset buffer size
- Use SOQL for loops instead of loading all data
- Add more filtering early in transformation
- Use file-based temporary storage
- Reduce number of step copies

2. Database Connection Errors:

Error Messages:

Error connecting to database: Connection refused
Communications link failure
The last packet sent successfully to the server was 0 milliseconds ago
Unable to connect to the database
Timeout expired

Troubleshooting Steps:

1. Verify database is running:
   ping db-server.company.com
   telnet db-server.company.com 3306

2. Check credentials:
   - Username/password correct?
   - Account not locked?
   - Permissions granted?

3. Test connection in Spoon:
   Tools → Database → Explore
   Test connection

4. Check firewall:
   - Port open?
   - IP whitelisted?

5. Verify connection string:
   jdbc:mysql://host:3306/database
   jdbc:postgresql://host:5432/database
   jdbc:oracle:thin:@host:1521:SID

Solutions:

Connection Parameters:
- Add timeout parameters:
  connectTimeout=30000
  socketTimeout=60000

- Enable connection pooling:
  Use connection pooling: Yes
  Test on borrow: Yes
  Test query: SELECT 1

- Implement retry logic:
  [Table Input]
      ↓ (Retry on failure)
  [Wait 30 seconds]
      ↓
  [Retry (3 attempts max)]

3. Row Metadata Errors:

Error Messages:

Unable to continue because of meta-data inconsistencies
Stream lookup column [field_name] not found in stream
Field [field_name] not found in row

Causes:

  • Field names don't match
  • Data types incompatible
  • Missing fields
  • Case sensitivity issues

Solutions:

1. Preview steps to see actual field names
2. Use Select Values to standardize field names
3. Check data types compatibility
4. Use Calculator or formulas to convert types

Example Fix:
[Input]
    ↓
[Select Values]  ← Rename and retype fields
  customer_ID → customer_id (lowercase)
  amount (String) → amount (Number)
    ↓
[Stream Lookup]  ← Now matches

4. File Not Found Errors:

Error Messages:

Unable to open file [filename.csv]
File does not exist
Access is denied
The system cannot find the path specified

Troubleshooting:

1. Verify file path:
   - Absolute vs relative paths
   - Forward slashes vs backslashes
   - Case sensitivity (Linux)

2. Check permissions:
   ls -la /path/to/file  # Linux
   icacls C:\path\to\file  # Windows

3. Verify file exists:
   [Check Files Exist]
       ↓ (Exists)
   [Process File]
       ↓ (Not Exists)
   [Send Alert]

4. Handle wildcards correctly:
   /data/sales_*.csv  ← Correct
   /data/sales_*.CSV  ← May fail on Linux (case-sensitive)

5. Step Errors:

Error Messages:

Couldn't find row origin
Unexpected error
Step [step_name] has stopped
Error converting data type
Divide by zero error

Debugging Approach:

1. Enable row-level logging:
   - Transformation settings → Logging
   - Log level: Detailed or Debug

2. Preview data at each step:
   - Right-click step → Preview
   - Check data and metadata

3. Add dummy output:
   [Problem Step]
       ↓
   [Text File Output: /tmp/debug.csv]
   (Examine output for issues)

4. Check for:
   - Null values
   - Data type mismatches
   - Invalid calculations
   - Missing references

6. Performance Issues:

Symptoms:

- Transformation runs very slow
- High CPU usage
- High memory usage
- Database locks
- Timeout errors

Diagnosis:

1. Check metrics:
   View → Metrics
   - Identify slow steps
   - Check rows per second
   - Monitor memory usage

2. Enable step metrics:
   - Transformation settings → Miscellaneous
   - Step performance monitoring: Yes

3. Profile transformation:
   - Run with detailed logging
   - Analyze log for bottlenecks
   - Check database query performance

Solutions:

1. Optimize SQL queries:
   - Add WHERE clauses
   - Create indexes
   - Use EXPLAIN to analyze

2. Reduce data volume:
   - Filter early
   - Select only needed columns
   - Process incrementally

3. Parallel processing:
   - Increase step copies
   - Use clustering
   - Partition data

4. Database tuning:
   - Increase batch size
   - Use connection pooling
   - Optimize commit frequency

7. Encoding Issues:

Error Messages:

Invalid byte sequence for encoding
Malformed input
Character encoding error
Invalid UTF-8 sequence

Solutions:

Text File Input:
- Encoding: UTF-8 (or appropriate encoding)
- Try different encodings if issues persist:
  * UTF-8
  * ISO-8859-1
  * Windows-1252
  * UTF-16

Detect encoding:
file -i filename.csv  # Linux

8. Date/Time Errors:

Error Messages:

Error converting date
Invalid date format
Unparseable date
Date out of range

Solutions:

Calculator or Select Values:
- Define date format explicitly:
  * yyyy-MM-dd
  * MM/dd/yyyy
  * dd-MMM-yyyy HH:mm:ss

- Use date conversion:
  [String] → [Calculator: String to Date] → [Date]

- Handle nulls:
  IF(ISNULL(date_field), '1900-01-01', date_field)

Logging and Debugging:

Enable Comprehensive Logging:

Transformation Settings → Logging:
- Log level: Detailed
- Log connection: File or Database
- Log file:
  /logs/trans_${INTERNAL.TRANSFORMATION.NAME}_${Internal.Job.Start.Date}.log

Job Settings → Logging:
- Log level: Detailed
- Log file:
  /logs/job_${INTERNAL.JOB.NAME}_${Internal.Job.Start.Date}.log

Log Analysis:

# Search for errors
grep -i "error" /logs/transformation.log

# Check step execution times
grep "Finished" /logs/transformation.log

# Find memory issues
grep -i "memory\|heap" /logs/transformation.log

# Check row counts
grep "read\|written" /logs/transformation.log

Debug Mode:

1. Set breakpoints:
   - Pause transformation at specific steps
   - Inspect data

2. Preview data:
   - Right-click step → Preview
   - Check sample rows

3. View step metrics:
   - View → Metrics
   - Monitor real-time performance

Common Pitfalls:

1. Not Testing with Real Data:

❌ Test with 100 rows

✅ Test with production-sized datasets

2. Ignoring Error Handling:

❌ No error hops configured

✅ Error handling for all critical steps

3. Hard-Coded Values:

❌ Paths, dates, credentials in transformation

✅ Use parameters and variables

4. No Logging:

❌ Minimal or no logging

✅ Detailed logging for production

Best Practices:

✅ Always preview data at each step

✅ Enable detailed logging during development

✅ Test with various data scenarios

✅ Implement proper error handling

✅ Monitor resource usage

✅ Document known issues and solutions

✅ Use version control

✅ Keep transformations simple and focused

✅ Test connection before processing

✅ Implement retry logic for transient errors

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How do you implement real-time data integration with PDI?
docs.text:
A: Real-time data integration in PDI involves continuous processing, event-driven architectures, and integration with streaming platforms.

Real-Time Patterns:

1. File Monitoring:

Job Pattern:
[Start]
    ↓
[Wait for File]
  - Watch directory: /input
  - File pattern: *.csv
  - Check interval: 5 seconds
    ↓ (File arrives)
[Process File Transformation]
    ↓
[Move to Processed]
    ↓
[Loop back to Wait for File]

Implementation:

Wait for File Entry:
- Filename/Directory: /input
- Wildcard: sales_*.csv
- Maximum timeout: 0 (wait indefinitely)
- Check cycle time: 5000 ms
- Success when file arrives: Yes
- Add filename to result: Yes

2. Database Change Data Capture (CDC):

Log-Based CDC:

-- Create change log table
CREATE TABLE customer_changes (
    change_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INTEGER,
    operation VARCHAR(10),  -- INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
    change_timestamp TIMESTAMP,
    old_values JSONB,
    new_values JSONB
);

-- Trigger to capture changes
CREATE TRIGGER customer_cdc_trigger
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON customers
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION log_customer_changes();

PDI Processing:

[Table Input: Read New Changes]
SELECT *
FROM customer_changes
WHERE change_id > ${LAST_PROCESSED_ID}
ORDER BY change_id
LIMIT 10000;
    ↓
[Switch/Case on Operation]
  ├─→ INSERT → [Process Insert]
  ├─→ UPDATE → [Process Update]
  └─→ DELETE → [Process Delete]
    ↓
[Update Last Processed ID]

3. Message Queue Integration:

Apache Kafka Integration:

Kafka Consumer Configuration:
- Bootstrap servers: kafka1:9092,kafka2:9092
- Topic: customer_events
- Group ID: pdi_consumer_group
- Auto offset reset: latest
- Enable auto commit: false
- Max poll records: 1000

Transformation:

[Kafka Consumer]
  - Topic: customer_events
  - Message format: JSON
    ↓
[JSON Input]
  - Parse JSON message
    ↓
[Process Event]
  - Transform data
  - Apply business rules
    ↓
[Table Output]
  - Write to target database
    ↓
[Kafka Consumer: Commit Offset]

4. REST API Polling:

[Start]
    ↓
[Loop]
    ↓
[REST Client]
  - URL: https://api.example.com/events
  - Method: GET
  - Parameters: since=${LAST_TIMESTAMP}
    ↓
[JSON Input]
  - Parse response
    ↓
[Filter New Events]
    ↓
[Process Events]
    ↓
[Update Last Timestamp]
    ↓
[Sleep 10 seconds]
    ↓
[Loop back]

5. Micro-Batch Processing:

Schedule: Every 5 minutes
[Start]
    ↓
[Check for New Data]
  - Query: SELECT COUNT(*) 
           FROM staging 
           WHERE processed = 'N'
    ↓ (If count > 0)
[Process Batch]
  - Read unprocessed records
  - Transform
  - Load to target
  - Mark as processed
    ↓
[Validate Results]
    ↓
[Send Metrics]

Performance Considerations:

1. Minimize Latency:

✅ Use stream processing
✅ Avoid blocking operations
✅ Minimize transformation steps
✅ Use in-memory lookups
✅ Optimize database operations

2. Handle Back Pressure:

Configuration:
- Buffer size: Smaller for real-time
- Commit frequency: More frequent
- Error handling: Non-blocking
- Retry logic: Exponential backoff

3. Monitoring:

Real-Time Metrics:
- Processing latency
- Throughput (records/second)
- Error rate
- Queue depth
- Resource utilization

Alert Thresholds:
- Latency > 10 seconds
- Error rate > 1%
- Queue depth > 10,000
- CPU > 80%
- Memory > 90%

Example: Real-Time Sales Processing:

Architecture:
[Point of Sale Systems]
    ↓ (REST API)
[API Gateway]
    ↓ (Kafka)
[Sales Topic]
    ↓ (PDI Kafka Consumer)
[PDI Transformation]
  ├─→ [Enrich with Customer Data]
  ├─→ [Calculate Metrics]
  └─→ [Apply Business Rules]
    ↓
[Multi-Target Output]
  ├─→ [Data Warehouse]
  ├─→ [Analytics Database]
  └─→ [Real-Time Dashboard]

Implementation:

Job: Real-Time Sales Processing
[Start]
    ↓
[While True]
    ↓
[Transformation: Process Sales]
  [Kafka Consumer: sales-events]
      ↓
  [JSON Input]
      ↓
  [Validate Data]
      ↓
  [Database Lookup: Customers]
      ↓
  [Calculator: Metrics]
      ↓
  [Multi-Target Output]
    ├─→ [DW Table Output]
    ├─→ [Analytics Output]
    └─→ [Dashboard API]
      ↓
  [Commit Kafka Offset]
    ↓
[Monitor Performance]
    ↓
[Sleep 100ms]
    ↓
[Loop]

Best Practices:

✅ Design for idempotency

✅ Implement proper error handling

✅ Use message acknowledgment

✅ Monitor performance metrics

✅ Implement circuit breakers

✅ Use connection pooling

✅ Log all processing

✅ Test with various load scenarios

✅ Implement health checks

✅ Plan for failover

docs.title: Q: What is Salesforce's multi-tenant architecture and how does it impact development?
docs.text:
A: Salesforce uses a multi-tenant architecture where multiple customers (tenants) share the same infrastructure, application code, and database while maintaining complete data isolation and security.

Key Architectural Components:

  • Application Layer: Shared codebase serving all customers
  • Metadata Layer: Custom configurations unique to each org
  • Data Layer: Logically separated data for each tenant
  • Trust Layer: Security, authentication, and authorization

Impact on Development:

  • Governor Limits: Enforced to prevent resource monopolization
  • No Direct Database Access: Use SOQL/SOSL instead of SQL
  • Metadata-Driven: Customizations via metadata, not core code changes
  • Automatic Upgrades: Three releases per year affect all orgs

Governor Limits Context:

⚠️ SOQL Queries: 100 per transaction (synchronous)

⚠️ DML Statements: 150 per transaction

⚠️ Heap Size: 6 MB (synchronous), 12 MB (asynchronous)

⚠️ CPU Time: 10,000 ms (synchronous), 60,000 ms (asynchronous)

Salesforce Edition Availability:

  • ✅ All editions run on multi-tenant architecture
  • ✅ Performance and limits consistent across editions
  • ✅ Sandbox environments mirror production architecture

Best Practices:

✅ Design for bulk operations from the start

✅ Monitor governor limits during development

✅ Use asynchronous processing for large data volumes

✅ Implement proper exception handling

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is the difference between Standard Objects, Custom Objects, and External Objects?
docs.text:
A: Salesforce provides different object types to handle various data storage needs, from pre-built entities to custom business requirements and external system integration.

Standard Objects:

  • Definition: Pre-built objects provided by Salesforce
  • Examples: Account, Contact, Opportunity, Lead, Case
  • Characteristics: Cannot be deleted, have standard fields and functionality
  • Customization: Can add custom fields, relationships, and business logic

Custom Objects:

  • Definition: User-created objects specific to business needs
  • Naming: End with __c suffix (e.g., Property__c)
  • Characteristics: Full control over fields, relationships, and security
  • Limits: Maximum 2,000 custom objects per org (Enterprise Edition and above)

External Objects:

  • Definition: Objects that map to data stored outside Salesforce
  • Technology: Uses Salesforce Connect (formerly Lightning Connect)
  • Naming: End with __x suffix (e.g., ExternalInventory__x)
  • Use Cases: Real-time access to external data without replication

Example: Creating a Custom Object Relationship

// Query custom object with standard object relationship
List<Property__c> properties = [
    SELECT Id, Name, Price__c, Account__r.Name, Account__r.BillingCity
    FROM Property__c
    WHERE Price__c > 500000 AND Account__r.Type = 'Customer'
    ORDER BY Price__c DESC
    LIMIT 100
];

for (Property__c prop : properties) {
    System.debug('Property: ' + prop.Name + 
                 ' - Owner: ' + prop.Account__r.Name);
}

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Custom Objects: 2,000 per org

⚠️ Custom Fields: 500 per object (Enterprise), 800 (Unlimited)

⚠️ External Objects: 100 per org with Salesforce Connect

⚠️ Relationships: 40 total relationships per object

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Professional Edition: Standard objects only
  • ✅ Enterprise Edition: Standard + Custom objects (up to 200)
  • ✅ Unlimited Edition: Standard + Custom objects (up to 2,000)
  • ✅ Salesforce Connect: Available with add-on license

When to Use Each:

  • Standard Objects: Core business processes (CRM, sales, service)
  • Custom Objects: Industry-specific or unique business needs
  • External Objects: Integration without data duplication

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is Salesforce's Order of Execution and why is it critical?
docs.text:
A: The Order of Execution is the sequence in which Salesforce executes automation, validation, and database operations when a record is saved. Understanding this order is critical for preventing conflicts and ensuring predictable behavior.

Complete Order of Execution:

  1. Load: Original record from database or initialize new record
  2. New Values: Overwrite with user-submitted values
  3. System Validation: Required fields, field formats, max length
  4. Before Triggers: Execute before save triggers
  5. Custom Validation Rules: User-defined validation logic
  6. Duplicate Rules: Check for duplicate records
  7. Save (Not Committed): Record saved to database but not committed
  8. After Triggers: Execute after save triggers
  9. Assignment Rules: Execute assignment rules (Leads, Cases)
  10. Auto-Response Rules: Send auto-response emails
  11. Workflow Rules: Execute workflow field updates
  12. Processes: Execute Process Builder processes
  13. Flows: Execute record-triggered flows
  14. Escalation Rules: Execute escalation rules (Cases)
  15. Roll-Up Summary Fields: Calculate roll-up summaries
  16. Criteria-Based Sharing: Recalculate sharing
  17. Commit: Commit all DML operations
  18. Post-Commit Logic: Execute after commit (async operations)

Critical Understanding for Each Role:

For Developers:

  • Before triggers fire before validation rules
  • After triggers see the committed data
  • Avoid recursive triggers by checking Trigger.isExecuting
  • Use trigger frameworks to control execution order

For Administrators:

  • Validation rules run after before triggers
  • Workflow field updates trigger another save operation
  • Process Builder and Flows run after workflows
  • Multiple automations can cause recursion

For Architects:

  • Design systems aware of multiple automation layers
  • Consider performance impact of cascading updates
  • Plan for governor limits in complex automation chains
  • Document execution flow for maintenance

Example: Proper Trigger Design

// Before Trigger - Set default values
trigger AccountTrigger on Account (before insert, before update) {
    for (Account acc : Trigger.new) {
        // Set defaults before validation
        if (acc.Industry == null) {
            acc.Industry = 'Other';
        }

        // Calculate derived fields
        if (acc.AnnualRevenue != null && acc.AnnualRevenue > 1000000) {
            acc.Rating = 'Hot';
        }
    }
}

// After Trigger - Create related records
trigger AccountTriggerAfter on Account (after insert, after update) {
    List<Task> tasksToCreate = new List<Task>();

    for (Account acc : Trigger.new) {
        if (acc.Rating == 'Hot' && Trigger.oldMap.get(acc.Id).Rating != 'Hot') {
            Task t = new Task(
                Subject = 'Follow up with hot account',
                WhatId = acc.Id,
                ActivityDate = Date.today().addDays(1),
                Status = 'Not Started',
                Priority = 'High'
            );
            tasksToCreate.add(t);
        }
    }

    if (!tasksToCreate.isEmpty()) {
        insert tasksToCreate;
    }
}

Common Pitfalls:

❌ SOQL queries inside before triggers for data already loaded

❌ Creating infinite loops with workflow field updates

❌ Mixing declarative and programmatic automation without coordination

❌ Not handling recursion in complex automation scenarios

Best Practices:

✅ Use before triggers for field updates on the same object

✅ Use after triggers for related object operations

✅ Implement trigger handler frameworks for maintainability

✅ Document all automation in your org

✅ Test with multiple automation layers active

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Total Trigger Execution: Counts toward transaction limits

⚠️ Recursive Triggers: Limited to prevent infinite loops

⚠️ CPU Time: All automation shares the 10-second limit

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is the difference between Profiles and Permission Sets?
docs.text:
A: Profiles and Permission Sets both control user access, but they serve different purposes in Salesforce's security model. Understanding when to use each is essential for scalable user management.

Profiles:

  • Assignment: Every user must have exactly one profile
  • Purpose: Define baseline permissions and settings
  • Control: Object permissions, field permissions, app access, administrative permissions
  • Limitation: Cannot be additive (one per user)
  • Best Use: Define minimum access requirements by job role

Permission Sets:

  • Assignment: Users can have multiple permission sets (0 to many)
  • Purpose: Grant additional permissions beyond profile
  • Control: Same permissions as profiles (additive only)
  • Benefit: More flexible than creating multiple profiles
  • Best Use: Grant temporary or role-specific access

Permission Set Groups (Winter '20+):

  • Purpose: Bundle multiple permission sets together
  • Assignment: Simplify permission management at scale
  • Muting: Ability to mute specific permissions within the group

Example Permission Strategy:

// Check user permissions programmatically
public class PermissionChecker {

    public static Boolean hasCustomPermission(String permissionName) {
        return FeatureManagement.checkPermission(permissionName);
    }

    public static Boolean canDeleteAccounts() {
        Schema.DescribeSObjectResult accountDescribe = Account.sObjectType.getDescribe();
        return accountDescribe.isDeletable();
    }

    public static Boolean hasFieldAccess(String objectName, String fieldName) {
        Schema.SObjectType objType = Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(objectName);
        Schema.DescribeSObjectResult objDescribe = objType.getDescribe();
        Map<String, Schema.SObjectField> fields = objDescribe.fields.getMap();
        Schema.DescribeFieldResult fieldDescribe = fields.get(fieldName).getDescribe();

        return fieldDescribe.isAccessible();
    }
}

Practical Scenarios:

Scenario 1: Sales Team Structure

  • Profile: Sales User (base access to Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities)
  • Permission Set 1: "Sales Manager" (additional report access, dashboard management)
  • Permission Set 2: "Contract Approver" (temporary access during Q4)

Scenario 2: Project-Based Access

  • Profile: Standard User (minimal access)
  • Permission Set: "Project Alpha Team" (access to custom Project Alpha objects)
  • Benefit: Easy to add/remove users from project without profile changes

Best Practices by Role:

For Administrators:

✅ Create minimal profiles with base access

✅ Use permission sets for additional access

✅ Name permission sets descriptively (e.g., "Billing_Team_Extended")

✅ Regular audit of permission set assignments

✅ Document permission strategy

For Architects:

✅ Design permission model for scalability

✅ Plan for org-wide permission set groups

✅ Consider Custom Permissions for feature flags

✅ Implement permission checking in code

✅ Plan for license type differences

Common Mistakes:

❌ Creating too many profiles (hard to maintain)

❌ Not using permission sets for temporary access

❌ Cloning standard profiles unnecessarily

❌ Granting "View All" and "Modify All" permissions liberally

❌ Not documenting permission strategy

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Professional Edition: Profiles only (no permission sets)
  • ✅ Enterprise Edition: Profiles + Permission Sets
  • ✅ Unlimited Edition: Profiles + Permission Sets + Permission Set Groups
  • ✅ Developer Edition: Full permission management available

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Permission Sets per User: 1,000 assignments (including via groups)

⚠️ Permission Set Groups: Included in the 1,000 limit

⚠️ Custom Permissions: 500 per org
