docs.title: Q: What are the different types of Salesforce APIs and when should each be used?
docs.text:
A: Salesforce provides multiple APIs for different integration scenarios. Each API has specific use cases, advantages, and limitations.

API Types:

REST API:

  • Use Case: Mobile and web applications, lightweight integrations
  • Data Format: JSON or XML
  • Authentication: OAuth 2.0
  • Best For: CRUD operations on records, flexible queries

SOAP API:

  • Use Case: Enterprise integrations, robust error handling
  • Data Format: XML
  • Authentication: Username/password or OAuth
  • Best For: Complex integrations requiring WSDL

Bulk API:

  • Use Case: Loading or deleting large data sets (thousands to millions of records)
  • Data Format: CSV, JSON, or XML
  • Best For: Data migration, large-scale data operations

Streaming API:

  • Use Case: Real-time event notifications
  • Protocol: Bayeux/CometD
  • Best For: Push notifications, real-time updates

Metadata API:

  • Use Case: Deploy and retrieve metadata (custom objects, fields, Apex, etc.)
  • Best For: CI/CD pipelines, sandbox refreshes

Tooling API:

  • Use Case: Build custom development tools
  • Best For: Debugging, code manipulation, metadata operations

REST API Example:

// Callout to external REST API
public class RestApiExample {

    @future(callout=true)
    public static void makeRestCallout() {
        Http http = new Http();
        HttpRequest request = new HttpRequest();

        request.setEndpoint('https://api.example.com/data');
        request.setMethod('GET');
        request.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
        request.setHeader('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + getAccessToken());
        request.setTimeout(120000); // 120 seconds

        HttpResponse response = http.send(request);

        if (response.getStatusCode() == 200) {
            String jsonResponse = response.getBody();
            System.debug('Response: ' + jsonResponse);

            // Parse JSON
            Map<String, Object> results = (Map<String, Object>) JSON.deserializeUntyped(jsonResponse);
            // Process results
        } else {
            System.debug('Error: ' + response.getStatus());
        }
    }

    // POST request
    public static void postData(String data) {
        Http http = new Http();
        HttpRequest request = new HttpRequest();

        request.setEndpoint('https://api.example.com/create');
        request.setMethod('POST');
        request.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
        request.setBody(data);

        HttpResponse response = http.send(request);
        System.debug('Status Code: ' + response.getStatusCode());
    }
}

SOAP API Example:

// Consuming external SOAP Web Service
public class SoapApiExample {

    public static void callExternalService() {
        // Generated from WSDL
        ExternalService.ServicePort port = new ExternalService.ServicePort();
        port.timeout_x = 120000;

        try {
            String result = port.someMethod('parameter');
            System.debug('Result: ' + result);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.debug('Error: ' + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Bulk API Pattern:

// Bulk API 2.0 usage
public class BulkApiExample {

    public static void bulkInsertAccounts(List<Account> accounts) {
        // Prepare CSV content
        String csvContent = 'Name,Industry,AnnualRevenue\n';
        for (Account acc : accounts) {
            csvContent += acc.Name + ',' + acc.Industry + ',' + acc.AnnualRevenue + '\n';
        }

        // Create bulk job
        HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest();
        req.setEndpoint(URL.getSalesforceBaseUrl().toExternalForm() + 
                       '/services/data/v60.0/jobs/ingest');
        req.setMethod('POST');
        req.setHeader('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + UserInfo.getSessionId());
        req.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');

        String jobBody = JSON.serialize(new Map<String, Object>{
            'operation' => 'insert',
            'object' => 'Account',
            'contentType' => 'CSV'
        });
        req.setBody(jobBody);

        Http http = new Http();
        HttpResponse res = http.send(req);

        // Handle response and upload data
    }
}

API Limits:

⚠️ REST API: 15,000 requests per 24 hours (may vary by edition)

⚠️ SOAP API: Same as REST API

⚠️ Bulk API: 10,000 batch operations per 24 hours

⚠️ Streaming API: 40 topics, 100,000 events per 24 hours

Best Practices:

✅ Use REST API for modern integrations

✅ Use Bulk API for large data volumes

✅ Implement retry logic for failed requests

✅ Use Named Credentials for authentication

✅ Handle rate limits gracefully

✅ Log all API interactions

✅ Implement proper error handling

API Decision Matrix:

Use REST API When:

  • Building mobile/web apps
  • Need real-time data access
  • Working with modern tech stack
  • Small to medium data volumes

Use SOAP API When:

  • Legacy system integration
  • Need strict typing (WSDL)
  • Complex transactions required
  • Enterprise service bus integration

Use Bulk API When:

  • Loading 50,000+ records
  • Data migration projects
  • Batch processing required
  • Performance is critical

Use Streaming API When:

  • Real-time notifications needed
  • Push-based architecture
  • Monitoring record changes
  • Event-driven integrations

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is the Salesforce Sharing Model and how does it work?
docs.text:
A: The Salesforce Sharing Model is a multi-layered security framework that controls record access. It follows the principle of least privilege, starting restrictive and opening access as needed.

Security Layers:

Layer 1: Organization-Wide Defaults (OWD):

  • Private: Only owner and above can access
  • Public Read Only: All users can view, only owner can edit
  • Public Read/Write: All users can view and edit
  • Controlled by Parent: For master-detail relationships

Layer 2: Role Hierarchy:

  • Users higher in hierarchy can access records owned by users below
  • Applies only when OWD is Private or Public Read Only
  • Does not apply to Contacts when OWD is Controlled by Parent

Layer 3: Sharing Rules:

  • Owner-Based: Share records based on owner
  • Criteria-Based: Share records based on field values
  • Grant additional access beyond OWD

Layer 4: Manual Sharing:

  • Owner can manually share individual records
  • Share button on record detail page
  • Temporary or permanent access

Layer 5: Apex Managed Sharing:

  • Programmatic sharing using Apex
  • Create, query, and delete share records
  • Most flexible but requires code

Sharing Model Example:

// Account Sharing Programmatically
public class AccountSharingService {

    // Share account with user
    public static void shareAccountWithUser(Id accountId, Id userId, String accessLevel) {
        AccountShare accShare = new AccountShare();
        accShare.AccountId = accountId;
        accShare.UserOrGroupId = userId;
        accShare.AccountAccessLevel = accessLevel; // 'Read', 'Edit'
        accShare.OpportunityAccessLevel = 'None'; // 'None', 'Read', 'Edit'
        accShare.CaseAccessLevel = 'None';
        accShare.RowCause = Schema.AccountShare.RowCause.Manual;

        try {
            insert accShare;
            System.debug('Account shared successfully');
        } catch (DmlException e) {
            System.debug('Error sharing account: ' + e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    // Remove manual sharing
    public static void removeAccountSharing(Id accountId, Id userId) {
        List<AccountShare> shares = [
            SELECT Id
            FROM AccountShare
            WHERE AccountId = :accountId
            AND UserOrGroupId = :userId
            AND RowCause = :Schema.AccountShare.RowCause.Manual
        ];

        if (!shares.isEmpty()) {
            delete shares;
        }
    }

    // Query account sharing
    public static List<AccountShare> getAccountSharing(Id accountId) {
        return [
            SELECT Id, AccountId, UserOrGroupId, AccountAccessLevel, RowCause
            FROM AccountShare
            WHERE AccountId = :accountId
        ];
    }

    // Bulk sharing
    public static void shareAccountsWithGroup(List<Id> accountIds, Id groupId) {
        List<AccountShare> sharesToCreate = new List<AccountShare>();

        for (Id accId : accountIds) {
            AccountShare accShare = new AccountShare();
            accShare.AccountId = accId;
            accShare.UserOrGroupId = groupId;
            accShare.AccountAccessLevel = 'Edit';
            accShare.OpportunityAccessLevel = 'Read';
            accShare.RowCause = Schema.AccountShare.RowCause.Manual;
            sharesToCreate.add(accShare);
        }

        if (!sharesToCreate.isEmpty()) {
            Database.SaveResult[] results = Database.insert(sharesToCreate, false);

            for (Database.SaveResult result : results) {
                if (!result.isSuccess()) {
                    System.debug('Error: ' + result.getErrors()[0].getMessage());
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Sharing with and without Sharing:

// Enforces sharing rules (default)
public with sharing class AccountController {
    public List<Account> getAccounts() {
        // Only returns accounts user has access to
        return [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account];
    }
}

// Ignores sharing rules (use cautiously)
public without sharing class AccountControllerNoSharing {
    public List<Account> getAllAccounts() {
        // Returns all accounts regardless of access
        return [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account];
    }
}

// Inherits sharing from calling class
public inherited sharing class AccountControllerInherited {
    public List<Account> getAccounts() {
        // Inherits sharing context from caller
        return [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account];
    }
}

// Mixed approach
public class AccountMixedSharing {

    // Respects sharing
    public with sharing List<Account> getUserVisibleAccounts() {
        return [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account];
    }

    // Helper class ignores sharing for specific operations
    private without sharing class InternalHelper {
        public List<Account> getAllAccounts() {
            return [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account];
        }
    }
}

Programmatic Sharing Patterns:

// Sharing based on custom logic
public class TerritorySharing {

    public static void shareAccountsWithTerritory(List<Account> accounts) {
        // Get territory assignments
        Map<Id, Set<Id>> accountToUsers = getTeritoryAssignments(accounts);

        List<AccountShare> shares = new List<AccountShare>();

        for (Id accountId : accountToUsers.keySet()) {
            for (Id userId : accountToUsers.get(accountId)) {
                AccountShare share = new AccountShare(
                    AccountId = accountId,
                    UserOrGroupId = userId,
                    AccountAccessLevel = 'Edit',
                    OpportunityAccessLevel = 'Edit',
                    RowCause = Schema.AccountShare.RowCause.Territory__c // Custom reason
                );
                shares.add(share);
            }
        }

        if (!shares.isEmpty()) {
            Database.insert(shares, false);
        }
    }

    private static Map<Id, Set<Id>> getTeritoryAssignments(List<Account> accounts) {
        Map<Id, Set<Id>> result = new Map<Id, Set<Id>>();
        // Logic to determine territory assignments
        return result;
    }
}

Security Best Practices:

✅ Always use "with sharing" unless there's a specific reason

✅ Never bypass sharing rules without security review

✅ Test with different user profiles

✅ Document security decisions

✅ Use Field-Level Security with sharing rules

✅ Audit sharing periodically

✅ Use Public Groups for easier maintenance

Common Sharing Scenarios:

// Scenario 1: Share with manager
public static void shareWithManager(Id recordId, Id ownerId) {
    User owner = [SELECT ManagerId FROM User WHERE Id = :ownerId];
    if (owner.ManagerId != null) {
        // Share logic
    }
}

// Scenario 2: Share with team members
public static void shareWithTeam(Id recordId, Id teamId) {
    Group team = [SELECT Id FROM Group WHERE Id = :teamId];
    // Share with public group
}

// Scenario 3: Expire sharing after date
public static void expireSharing() {
    List<AccountShare> expiredShares = [
        SELECT Id
        FROM AccountShare
        WHERE ExpirationDate__c < :Date.today()
    ];
    delete expiredShares;
}

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Sharing recalculation can be time-consuming

⚠️ Consider batch processing for large volumes

⚠️ Test with realistic data volumes

docs.title: Q: What are Salesforce Governor Limits and how do you write code to avoid hitting them?
docs.text:
A: Governor Limits are runtime limits enforced by Salesforce to ensure no single tenant monopolizes shared resources. Understanding and respecting these limits is fundamental to Apex development.

Critical Governor Limits:

Synchronous Limits (per transaction):

⚠️ Total SOQL Queries: 100

⚠️ Total SOQL Records Retrieved: 50,000

⚠️ Total DML Statements: 150

⚠️ Total DML Rows Processed: 10,000

⚠️ Total Heap Size: 6 MB

⚠️ Maximum CPU Time: 10,000 milliseconds

⚠️ Total Callouts: 100

Asynchronous Limits (per transaction):

⚠️ Total SOQL Queries: 200

⚠️ Total Heap Size: 12 MB

⚠️ Maximum CPU Time: 60,000 milliseconds

Bulkification Patterns:

❌ BAD: Non-Bulkified Code:

// NEVER DO THIS - SOQL in loop
trigger OpportunityTrigger on Opportunity (before insert) {
    for (Opportunity opp : Trigger.new) {
        // Query inside loop - will fail after 100 iterations
        Account acc = [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Id = :opp.AccountId];
        opp.Description = 'Account: ' + acc.Name;
    }
}

// NEVER DO THIS - DML in loop
trigger ContactTrigger on Contact (after insert) {
    for (Contact con : Trigger.new) {
        // DML inside loop - will fail after 150 iterations
        Task t = new Task(
            WhoId = con.Id,
            Subject = 'Follow up'
        );
        insert t;
    }
}

✅ GOOD: Bulkified Code:

// Bulkified SOQL
trigger OpportunityTrigger on Opportunity (before insert) {
    // Collect all Account IDs
    Set<Id> accountIds = new Set<Id>();
    for (Opportunity opp : Trigger.new) {
        if (opp.AccountId != null) {
            accountIds.add(opp.AccountId);
        }
    }

    // Single SOQL query outside loop
    Map<Id, Account> accountMap = new Map<Id, Account>(
        [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Id IN :accountIds]
    );

    // Use queried data
    for (Opportunity opp : Trigger.new) {
        if (opp.AccountId != null && accountMap.containsKey(opp.AccountId)) {
            Account acc = accountMap.get(opp.AccountId);
            opp.Description = 'Account: ' + acc.Name;
        }
    }
}

// Bulkified DML
trigger ContactTrigger on Contact (after insert) {
    // Collect all tasks in a list
    List<Task> tasksToInsert = new List<Task>();

    for (Contact con : Trigger.new) {
        tasksToInsert.add(new Task(
            WhoId = con.Id,
            Subject = 'Follow up with ' + con.FirstName
        ));
    }

    // Single DML operation outside loop
    if (!tasksToInsert.isEmpty()) {
        insert tasksToInsert;
    }
}

SOQL Best Practices:

public class SOQLOptimization {

    // Use selective queries
    public static List<Account> getHighValueAccounts() {
        // ✅ GOOD: Selective filter on indexed field
        return [
            SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue
            FROM Account
            WHERE AnnualRevenue > 1000000
            AND CreatedDate = LAST_N_DAYS:30
            LIMIT 10000
        ];
    }

    // Query only needed fields
    public static List<Account> getAccountNames() {
        // ✅ GOOD: Only query fields you need
        return [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account];

        // ❌ BAD: Don't query all fields
        // return [SELECT FIELDS(ALL) FROM Account];
    }

    // Use relationship queries efficiently
    public static List<Account> getAccountsWithContacts() {
        // ✅ GOOD: Single query with subquery
        return [
            SELECT Id, Name,
                   (SELECT Id, FirstName, LastName FROM Contacts LIMIT 5)
            FROM Account
            WHERE Type = 'Customer'
            LIMIT 100
        ];
    }

    // SOQL For Loops for large datasets
    public static void processLargeDataset() {
        // ✅ GOOD: Processes in batches of 200
        for (List<Account> accounts : [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account]) {
            // Process batch
            for (Account acc : accounts) {
                // Processing logic
            }
        }
    }

    // Avoid query all rows
    public static void queryWithLimit() {
        // ✅ GOOD: Use LIMIT
        List<Account> accounts = [SELECT Id FROM Account LIMIT 50000];

        // ❌ BAD: ALL ROWS can exceed limits
        // List<Account> accounts = [SELECT Id FROM Account ALL ROWS];
    }
}

DML Best Practices:

public class DMLOptimization {

    // Bulkify DML operations
    public static void bulkInsert(List<Account> accounts) {
        // ✅ GOOD: Single DML statement
        if (!accounts.isEmpty()) {
            insert accounts;
        }
    }

    // Use Database methods for partial success
    public static void partialSuccessInsert(List<Account> accounts) {
        // ✅ GOOD: Allows partial success
        Database.SaveResult[] results = Database.insert(accounts, false);

        for (Database.SaveResult result : results) {
            if (!result.isSuccess()) {
                for (Database.Error error : result.getErrors()) {
                    System.debug('Error: ' + error.getMessage());
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // Upsert for efficiency
    public static void upsertRecords(List<Account> accounts) {
        // ✅ GOOD: Single operation instead of query + insert/update
        upsert accounts Account.ExternalId__c;
    }

    // Update only changed records
    public static void updateChangedRecords(List<Account> newAccounts, Map<Id, Account> oldAccounts) {
        List<Account> accountsToUpdate = new List<Account>();

        for (Account acc : newAccounts) {
            Account oldAcc = oldAccounts.get(acc.Id);
            if (acc.AnnualRevenue != oldAcc.AnnualRevenue) {
                accountsToUpdate.add(acc);
            }
        }

        // ✅ GOOD: Only update records that changed
        if (!accountsToUpdate.isEmpty()) {
            update accountsToUpdate;
        }
    }
}

Heap Size Optimization:

public class HeapOptimization {

    // Use selective queries to reduce memory
    public static void processRecords() {
        // ✅ GOOD: Query only needed fields
        List<Account> accounts = [
            SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue
            FROM Account
            WHERE CreatedDate = THIS_YEAR
        ];

        // ❌ BAD: Querying all fields uses more heap
        // List<Account> accounts = [SELECT FIELDS(ALL) FROM Account];
    }

    // Process in batches
    public static void processBatches() {
        // ✅ GOOD: SOQL for loop processes in batches
        for (List<Account> batch : [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account]) {
            // Each batch frees memory after processing
            processAccountBatch(batch);
        }
    }

    private static void processAccountBatch(List<Account> accounts) {
        // Process batch
        List<Contact> contacts = new List<Contact>();
        for (Account acc : accounts) {
            contacts.add(new Contact(
                AccountId = acc.Id,
                LastName = 'Contact'
            ));
        }
        insert contacts;

        // Clear list to free memory
        contacts.clear();
    }

    // Avoid holding large strings
    public static void avoidLargeStrings() {
        // ❌ BAD: Building large strings in memory
        String largeString = '';
        for (Integer i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
            largeString += 'data' + i + ',';
        }

        // ✅ GOOD: Use List and join
        List<String> dataList = new List<String>();
        for (Integer i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
            dataList.add('data' + i);
        }
        String result = String.join(dataList, ',');
    }
}

CPU Time Optimization:

public class CPUOptimization {

    // Avoid complex nested loops
    public static void avoidNestedLoops(List<Account> accounts, List<Contact> contacts) {
        // ❌ BAD: O(n²) complexity
        for (Account acc : accounts) {
            for (Contact con : contacts) {
                if (con.AccountId == acc.Id) {
                    // Process
                }
            }
        }

        // ✅ GOOD: Use Map for O(n) complexity
        Map<Id, List<Contact>> contactsByAccount = new Map<Id, List<Contact>>();
        for (Contact con : contacts) {
            if (!contactsByAccount.containsKey(con.AccountId)) {
                contactsByAccount.put(con.AccountId, new List<Contact>());
            }
            contactsByAccount.get(con.AccountId).add(con);
        }

        for (Account acc : accounts) {
            List<Contact> accountContacts = contactsByAccount.get(acc.Id);
            if (accountContacts != null) {
                // Process
            }
        }
    }

    // Use efficient data structures
    public static void useEfficientStructures() {
        // ✅ GOOD: Set for uniqueness checks (O(1))
        Set<Id> accountIds = new Set<Id>();
        accountIds.add(someId);
        if (accountIds.contains(someId)) {
            // Found instantly
        }

        // ✅ GOOD: Map for lookups (O(1))
        Map<Id, Account> accountMap = new Map<Id, Account>();
        Account acc = accountMap.get(accountId);
    }

    // Avoid complex calculations in loops
    public static void optimizeCalculations(List<Account> accounts) {
        // ❌ BAD: Repeated calculation
        for (Account acc : accounts) {
            Decimal tax = acc.AnnualRevenue * getTaxRate();
        }

        // ✅ GOOD: Calculate once
        Decimal taxRate = getTaxRate();
        for (Account acc : accounts) {
            Decimal tax = acc.AnnualRevenue * taxRate;
        }
    }

    private static Decimal getTaxRate() {
        return 0.07;
    }
}

Monitoring Limits:

public class LimitMonitor {

    public static void logLimits(String context) {
        System.debug('=== GOVERNOR LIMITS: ' + context + ' ===');
        System.debug('SOQL Queries: ' + Limits.getQueries() + '/' + Limits.getLimitQueries());
        System.debug('Query Rows: ' + Limits.getQueryRows() + '/' + Limits.getLimitQueryRows());
        System.debug('DML Statements: ' + Limits.getDmlStatements() + '/' + Limits.getLimitDmlStatements());
        System.debug('DML Rows: ' + Limits.getDmlRows() + '/' + Limits.getLimitDmlRows());
        System.debug('CPU Time: ' + Limits.getCpuTime() + '/' + Limits.getLimitCpuTime());
        System.debug('Heap Size: ' + Limits.getHeapSize() + '/' + Limits.getLimitHeapSize());
        System.debug('Callouts: ' + Limits.getCallouts() + '/' + Limits.getLimitCallouts());
    }

    public static Boolean isApproachingLimit(Integer current, Integer max, Integer threshold) {
        return (current * 100 / max) > threshold;
    }
}

// Usage
LimitMonitor.logLimits('Before Processing');
// Processing logic
LimitMonitor.logLimits('After Processing');

if (LimitMonitor.isApproachingLimit(Limits.getQueries(), Limits.getLimitQueries(), 80)) {
    System.debug('WARNING: Approaching SOQL query limit');
}

Best Practices Summary:

✅ Always bulkify code (design for 200 records)

✅ Use SOQL For Loops for large datasets

✅ Query only needed fields

✅ Use selective SOQL queries

✅ Collect IDs, query once, process with Map

✅ Use efficient data structures (Set, Map)

✅ Monitor limits during development

✅ Test with realistic data volumes

✅ Consider asynchronous processing for large operations

✅ Use Database methods for partial success scenarios

docs.title: Q: What are common Apex exceptions and how do you handle them?
docs.text:
A: Proper exception handling is critical for robust Apex code. Understanding common exceptions and implementing appropriate error handling patterns ensures better code quality and user experience.

Common Apex Exceptions:

DmlException:

// Occurs during DML operations
try {
    Account acc = new Account(); // Missing required Name field
    insert acc;
} catch (DmlException e) {
    System.debug('DML Exception occurred');
    System.debug('Message: ' + e.getMessage());
    System.debug('Type: ' + e.getDmlType(0)); // INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
    System.debug('Fields: ' + e.getDmlFieldNames(0));
    System.debug('Status Code: ' + e.getDmlStatusCode(0));

    // Handle error
    for (Integer i = 0; i < e.getNumDml(); i++) {
        System.debug('Record ' + i + ': ' + e.getDmlMessage(i));
    }
}

QueryException:

// Occurs when query returns unexpected results
try {
    // SOQL with LIMIT 1 and expecting exactly one record
    Account acc = [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Name = 'NonExistent' LIMIT 1];
} catch (QueryException e) {
    System.debug('Query Exception: ' + e.getMessage());
    // Handle: List is empty or too many rows
}

// Better approach: Check list size
List<Account> accounts = [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Name = :searchName];
if (accounts.isEmpty()) {
    System.debug('No accounts found');
} else if (accounts.size() == 1) {
    Account acc = accounts[0];
} else {
    System.debug('Multiple accounts found');
}

NullPointerException:

// Occurs when accessing null object
try {
    Account acc = null;
    String name = acc.Name; // NullPointerException
} catch (NullPointerException e) {
    System.debug('Null Pointer Exception: ' + e.getMessage());
}

// Better approach: Null checking
Account acc = getAccount();
if (acc != null && String.isNotBlank(acc.Name)) {
    String name = acc.Name;
}

// Safe navigation (if available)
String name = acc?.Name;

ListException:

// Occurs with list index out of bounds
try {
    List<Account> accounts = new List<Account>();
    Account acc = accounts[0]; // ListException
} catch (ListException e) {
    System.debug('List Exception: ' + e.getMessage());
}

// Better approach: Check size
if (!accounts.isEmpty()) {
    Account acc = accounts[0];
}

MathException:

// Occurs with mathematical operations
try {
    Decimal result = 10 / 0; // Division by zero
} catch (MathException e) {
    System.debug('Math Exception: ' + e.getMessage());
}

// Better approach: Validate before operation
if (divisor != 0) {
    Decimal result = dividend / divisor;
}

CalloutException:

// Occurs during HTTP callouts
try {
    Http http = new Http();
    HttpRequest request = new HttpRequest();
    request.setEndpoint('https://api.example.com/data');
    request.setMethod('GET');
    request.setTimeout(120000);

    HttpResponse response = http.send(request);
} catch (CalloutException e) {
    System.debug('Callout Exception: ' + e.getMessage());
    // Handle network errors, timeouts, etc.
}

Comprehensive Exception Handling Pattern:

public class RobustExceptionHandling {

    public static void processAccounts(List<Account> accounts) {
        // Validate input
        if (accounts == null || accounts.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException('Account list cannot be null or empty');
        }

        Savepoint sp = Database.setSavepoint();

        try {
            // Step 1: Query related data
            Set<Id> accountIds = new Set<Id>();
            for (Account acc : accounts) {
                accountIds.add(acc.Id);
            }

            Map<Id, List<Contact>> contactsByAccount = queryContacts(accountIds);

            // Step 2: Process accounts
            List<Contact> contactsToUpdate = new List<Contact>();

            for (Account acc : accounts) {
                try {
                    // Process individual account
                    processAccount(acc, contactsByAccount.get(acc.Id));
                } catch (Exception e) {
                    // Log but continue processing other accounts
                    logError('Error processing account ' + acc.Id, e);
                }
            }

            // Step 3: Save changes
            if (!contactsToUpdate.isEmpty()) {
                Database.SaveResult[] results = Database.update(contactsToUpdate, false);
                handleSaveResults(results, contactsToUpdate);
            }

        } catch (QueryException e) {
            Database.rollback(sp);
            throw new ProcessingException('Query failed: ' + e.getMessage(), e);
        } catch (DmlException e) {
            Database.rollback(sp);
            throw new ProcessingException('DML failed: ' + e.getMessage(), e);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            Database.rollback(sp);
            throw new ProcessingException('Unexpected error: ' + e.getMessage(), e);
        } finally {
            // Cleanup code (always executes)
            System.debug('Processing completed');
            LimitMonitor.logLimits('After processAccounts');
        }
    }

    private static Map<Id, List<Contact>> queryContacts(Set<Id> accountIds) {
        Map<Id, List<Contact>> result = new Map<Id, List<Contact>>();

        List<Contact> contacts = [
            SELECT Id, AccountId, FirstName, LastName, Email
            FROM Contact
            WHERE AccountId IN :accountIds
        ];

        for (Contact con : contacts) {
            if (!result.containsKey(con.AccountId)) {
                result.put(con.AccountId, new List<Contact>());
            }
            result.get(con.AccountId).add(con);
        }

        return result;
    }

    private static void processAccount(Account acc, List<Contact> contacts) {
        if (acc == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException('Account cannot be null');
        }

        // Processing logic
        if (contacts != null && !contacts.isEmpty()) {
            for (Contact con : contacts) {
                // Process contact
            }
        }
    }

    private static void handleSaveResults(Database.SaveResult[] results, List<Contact> contacts) {
        for (Integer i = 0; i < results.size(); i++) {
            Database.SaveResult result = results[i];

            if (!result.isSuccess()) {
                Contact failedContact = contacts[i];
                System.debug('Failed to update Contact ' + failedContact.Id);

                for (Database.Error error : result.getErrors()) {
                    System.debug('Error: ' + error.getMessage());
                    System.debug('Fields: ' + error.getFields());
                    System.debug('Status: ' + error.getStatusCode());
                }
            }
        }
    }

    private static void logError(String message, Exception e) {
        System.debug(LoggingLevel.ERROR, '### ERROR: ' + message);
        System.debug(LoggingLevel.ERROR, '### Exception Type: ' + e.getTypeName());
        System.debug(LoggingLevel.ERROR, '### Message: ' + e.getMessage());
        System.debug(LoggingLevel.ERROR, '### Stack Trace: ' + e.getStackTraceString());
        System.debug(LoggingLevel.ERROR, '### Line Number: ' + e.getLineNumber());

        // Optionally log to custom object for tracking
        createErrorLog(message, e);
    }

    private static void createErrorLog(String message, Exception e) {
        Error_Log__c log = new Error_Log__c(
            Message__c = message,
            Exception_Type__c = e.getTypeName(),
            Exception_Message__c = e.getMessage(),
            Stack_Trace__c = e.getStackTraceString(),
            Line_Number__c = e.getLineNumber(),
            Timestamp__c = DateTime.now()
        );

        try {
            insert log;
        } catch (Exception insertException) {
            // If logging fails, just debug
            System.debug('Failed to create error log: ' + insertException.getMessage());
        }
    }

    // Custom exception classes
    public class ProcessingException extends Exception {}
    public class IllegalArgumentException extends Exception {}
}

Exception Best Practices:

Try-Catch-Finally Pattern:

public void robustMethod() {
    Savepoint sp = Database.setSavepoint();

    try {
        // Main logic here
        processData();
    } catch (DmlException e) {
        // Handle DML errors specifically
        Database.rollback(sp);
        handleDmlException(e);
    } catch (QueryException e) {
        // Handle query errors
        Database.rollback(sp);
        handleQueryException(e);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        // Catch-all for unexpected errors
        Database.rollback(sp);
        handleGenericException(e);
    } finally {
        // Always executes (cleanup)
        cleanup();
    }
}

Custom Exceptions:

public class ValidationException extends Exception {}
public class InsufficientDataException extends Exception {}
public class BusinessLogicException extends Exception {}

// Usage
public void validateAccount(Account acc) {
    if (String.isBlank(acc.Name)) {
        throw new ValidationException('Account Name is required');
    }

    if (acc.AnnualRevenue == null || acc.AnnualRevenue <= 0) {
        throw new ValidationException('Annual Revenue must be positive');
    }
}

Error Messages for Users:

public class UserFriendlyErrors {

    public static void handleUserError(Exception e) {
        String userMessage;
        String technicalMessage = e.getMessage();

        if (e instanceof DmlException) {
            DmlException dmlEx = (DmlException) e;
            if (dmlEx.getDmlType(0) == StatusCode.REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING) {
                userMessage = 'Please fill in all required fields.';
            } else if (dmlEx.getDmlType(0) == StatusCode.DUPLICATE_VALUE) {
                userMessage = 'A record with this value already exists.';
            } else {
                userMessage = 'Unable to save record. Please contact support.';
            }
        } else if (e instanceof QueryException) {
            userMessage = 'No records found matching your criteria.';
        } else {
            userMessage = 'An unexpected error occurred. Please try again.';
        }

        // Show user-friendly message
        ApexPages.addMessage(new ApexPages.Message(
            ApexPages.Severity.ERROR,
            userMessage
        ));

        // Log technical details
        System.debug('Technical error: ' + technicalMessage);
        System.debug('Stack trace: ' + e.getStackTraceString());
    }
}

Best Practices:

✅ Catch specific exceptions before general Exception

✅ Always include cleanup code in finally block

✅ Log all exceptions with full context

✅ Provide user-friendly error messages

✅ Use custom exceptions for business logic errors

✅ Implement savepoints for rollback capability

✅ Never catch exceptions without handling them

✅ Don't expose technical details to end users

❌ Don't use empty catch blocks

❌ Don't catch Exception without logging

❌ Don't ignore errors silently

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What are the key topics and exam details for Platform Developer I Certification?
docs.text:
A: The Salesforce Certified Platform Developer I credential is designed for developers with knowledge, skills, and experience building custom applications on the Lightning Platform.

Exam Details:

Format:

  • Questions: 60 multiple-choice/multiple-select
  • Duration: 105 minutes
  • Passing Score: 68% (41 correct answers)
  • Registration Fee: $200 USD (plus applicable taxes)
  • Retake Fee: $100 USD (plus applicable taxes)
  • Delivery: Proctored online or onsite

Exam Outline (% of Exam):

1. Salesforce Fundamentals (7%):

  • Understand platform capabilities and development models
  • Navigate and use Developer Console, Developer tools
  • Identify common use cases for formulas, validations, automation

Key Concepts:

  • Multi-tenant architecture
  • Metadata-driven development
  • Declarative vs Programmatic customization
  • MVC architecture in Salesforce
  • Order of execution

2. Data Modeling and Management (13%):

  • Describe capabilities of core standard objects
  • Create appropriate relationships between objects
  • Describe capabilities of standard and custom fields
  • Understand implications of field data types

Key Concepts:

  • Standard objects (Account, Contact, Opportunity, etc.)
  • Custom objects and fields
  • Lookup vs Master-Detail relationships
  • External objects
  • Field data types and their impacts
  • Schema builder

3. Logic and Process Automation (38%):

  • Write Apex triggers and classes
  • Describe capabilities of formula fields
  • Implement exception handling
  • Understand governor limits
  • Write SOQL and SOSL queries
  • Implement asynchronous Apex

Key Concepts:

// Apex Triggers
trigger AccountTrigger on Account (before insert, after update) {
    if (Trigger.isBefore && Trigger.isInsert) {
        for (Account acc : Trigger.new) {
            // Before insert logic
        }
    }
}

// Apex Classes
public class AccountService {
    public static List<Account> getHighValueAccounts() {
        return [SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE AnnualRevenue > 1000000];
    }
}

// Exception Handling
try {
    insert accounts;
} catch (DmlException e) {
    System.debug('Error: ' + e.getMessage());
}

// Asynchronous Apex
@future
public static void processAsync(Set<Id> accountIds) {
    // Asynchronous processing
}

4. User Interface (14%):

  • Create Lightning Web Components
  • Understand Lightning component structure
  • Implement communication patterns
  • Describe capabilities of Visualforce

Key Concepts:

// Lightning Web Component
import { LightningElement, api, wire } from 'lwc';
import getAccounts from '@salesforce/apex/AccountController.getAccounts';

export default class AccountList extends LightningElement {
    @api recordId;

    @wire(getAccounts)
    accounts;
}

5. Testing, Debugging, and Deployment (16%):

  • Write and execute test classes
  • Understand deployment methods
  • Debug Apex code
  • Describe deployment tools

Key Concepts:

@isTest
private class AccountServiceTest {
    @TestSetup
    static void setup() {
        // Test data setup
    }

    @isTest
    static void testGetHighValueAccounts() {
        Test.startTest();
        List<Account> accounts = AccountService.getHighValueAccounts();
        Test.stopTest();

        System.assertEquals(5, accounts.size());
    }
}

6. Integration (12%):

  • Implement REST and SOAP callouts
  • Describe capabilities of Salesforce APIs
  • Understand authentication mechanisms

Study Resources:

Official Salesforce:

  • Exam Guide
  • Trailmix for Platform Developer I

Trailhead Modules:

  • Apex Basics & Database
  • Apex Triggers
  • Asynchronous Apex
  • Lightning Web Components
  • Developer Console Basics
  • Testing in Apex

Practice Projects:

  • Build custom objects and relationships
  • Write triggers with handler pattern
  • Create Lightning Web Components
  • Implement test classes with >75% coverage
  • Practice SOQL queries
  • Build REST API integrations

Key Study Tips:

✅ Complete all recommended Trailhead modules

✅ Get hands-on experience in Developer Edition org

✅ Practice writing Apex code daily

✅ Understand governor limits thoroughly

✅ Master trigger and test class patterns

✅ Know when to use declarative vs programmatic

✅ Understand asynchronous Apex patterns

✅ Practice debugging with Developer Console

Common Exam Topics:

Apex Topics:

  • Trigger context variables
  • Collections (List, Set, Map)
  • SOQL queries and relationships
  • DML operations
  • Exception handling
  • Governor limits
  • Asynchronous Apex (@future, Batch, Queueable, Schedulable)

Lightning Topics:

  • Component lifecycle hooks
  • Decorators (@api, @track, @wire)
  • Communication patterns
  • Lightning Data Service
  • Event handling

Testing Topics:

  • Test class structure
  • @TestSetup
  • Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest()
  • System.runAs()
  • Mock callouts
  • Code coverage requirements

Sample Questions Style:

Question: Which governor limit is most likely to be exceeded when processing large datasets?

A) SOQL queries per transaction (100)

B) DML statements per transaction (150)

C) SOQL records retrieved per transaction (50,000)

D) Heap size (6 MB)

Answer: C - Large dataset processing often exceeds the 50,000 record retrieval limit

Question: What is the correct way to bulkify this code?

for (Account acc : accounts) {
    List<Contact> cons = [SELECT Id FROM Contact WHERE AccountId = :acc.Id];
}

Answer: Query all contacts in one SOQL statement using WHERE AccountId IN :accountIds

docs.title: Q: What is Salesforce Sales Cloud and what are its core capabilities?
docs.text:
A: Sales Cloud is Salesforce's flagship product designed to help sales teams manage the entire sales process from lead generation to closing deals and beyond. It provides tools for managing customer relationships, tracking sales activities, and forecasting revenue.

Core Capabilities:

  • Lead Management: Capture, qualify, and convert leads into opportunities
  • Opportunity Management: Track deals through the sales pipeline
  • Account & Contact Management: Maintain customer relationship data
  • Activity Management: Log calls, emails, meetings, and tasks
  • Sales Forecasting: Predict revenue and track quota attainment
  • Reports & Dashboards: Visualize sales performance and metrics
  • Sales Collaboration: Enable team selling with Chatter and Slack integration
  • Mobile Access: Manage sales activities on-the-go

Key Objects in Sales Cloud:

  • Lead: Potential customer who hasn't been qualified yet
  • Account: Company or organization you do business with
  • Contact: Individual person associated with an Account
  • Opportunity: Qualified sales deal in your pipeline
  • Quote: Pricing proposal sent to customers
  • Product: Items or services your company sells
  • Price Book: Lists of products with pricing information

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Essentials: Basic sales features for up to 10 users
  • ✅ Professional: Complete CRM with workflow and API access
  • ✅ Enterprise: Advanced customization, multiple sales processes
  • ✅ Unlimited: Premium features with unlimited support

Use Cases:

  • B2B sales teams managing complex sales cycles
  • Inside sales teams with high-velocity lead conversion
  • Field sales representatives tracking customer interactions
  • Sales managers forecasting and managing team performance

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is the Lead-to-Cash process in Sales Cloud?
docs.text:
A: The Lead-to-Cash process represents the complete sales lifecycle in Salesforce, from initial prospect identification through deal closure and revenue recognition.

Process Stages:

  • Lead Generation: Marketing campaigns generate leads
  • Lead Qualification: Sales team qualifies lead interest and fit
  • Lead Conversion: Convert qualified lead to Account, Contact, and Opportunity
  • Opportunity Management: Progress deal through sales stages
  • Quote Creation: Generate pricing proposals
  • Contract Negotiation: Finalize terms and conditions
  • Deal Closure: Win the opportunity and create order
  • Order Fulfillment: Process order and deliver products/services
  • Revenue Recognition: Record revenue in financial systems

Lead Conversion Process:

// Example: Convert Lead programmatically
Lead leadToConvert = [SELECT Id, FirstName, LastName, Company, Email 
                      FROM Lead 
                      WHERE Id = :leadId];

Database.LeadConvert lc = new Database.LeadConvert();
lc.setLeadId(leadToConvert.Id);

// Create new Account and Contact
lc.setDoNotCreateOpportunity(false); // Create Opportunity
lc.setConvertedStatus('Qualified'); // Lead Status after conversion

// Perform conversion
Database.LeadConvertResult lcr = Database.convertLead(lc);

if (lcr.isSuccess()) {
    System.debug('Lead converted successfully');
    System.debug('Account ID: ' + lcr.getAccountId());
    System.debug('Contact ID: ' + lcr.getContactId());
    System.debug('Opportunity ID: ' + lcr.getOpportunityId());
}

Key Considerations:

  • Lead Assignment: Use lead assignment rules for automatic routing
  • Duplicate Prevention: Check for existing Accounts before conversion
  • Required Fields: Ensure all required fields are populated
  • Conversion Mapping: Map custom lead fields to Account/Contact/Opportunity fields

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 15 DML operations can occur during lead conversion

⚠️ Cannot convert leads with unresolved duplicate alerts in certain configurations

Best Practices:

✅ Define clear lead qualification criteria

✅ Use validation rules to ensure data quality before conversion

✅ Map custom fields to preserve data during conversion

✅ Implement duplicate management to prevent redundant records

✅ Track conversion metrics to optimize sales process

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is the difference between a Lead and a Contact in Sales Cloud?
docs.text:
A: Understanding the distinction between Leads and Contacts is crucial for proper data management and sales process execution in Salesforce.

Lead:

  • Definition: Unqualified prospect who has shown interest but not yet vetted
  • Purpose: Track potential customers before qualifying them
  • Status: Not yet determined to be a viable sales opportunity
  • Conversion: Can be converted to Account, Contact, and Opportunity
  • Use Case: Marketing campaigns, trade shows, website inquiries

Contact:

  • Definition: Qualified person associated with an Account
  • Purpose: Maintain relationships with customers and prospects
  • Status: Already qualified and in your CRM system
  • Relationship: Must be related to an Account
  • Use Case: Existing customers, partners, qualified prospects

Key Differences:

  • Qualification Status: Leads are unqualified, Contacts are qualified
  • Account Association: Leads standalone, Contacts require Account
  • Data Model: Different objects with separate fields and processes
  • Lifecycle: Leads convert to Contacts, Contacts don't convert
  • Duplicates: Can have same person as both Lead and Contact

Lead Conversion Process:

When a Lead is converted, Salesforce automatically:

  • Creates a new Account (or associates with existing)
  • Creates a new Contact
  • Optionally creates an Opportunity
  • Transfers Lead custom fields to corresponding objects
  • Changes Lead status to "Converted"

Example - Lead Qualification:

// Query leads ready for conversion
List<Lead> qualifiedLeads = [
    SELECT Id, FirstName, LastName, Company, Email, 
           Phone, LeadSource, Rating
    FROM Lead
    WHERE Status = 'Qualified'
    AND Rating = 'Hot'
    AND Email != null
    ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC
    LIMIT 200
];

// Check for duplicates before conversion
for (Lead l : qualifiedLeads) {
    List<Contact> existingContacts = [
        SELECT Id, AccountId 
        FROM Contact 
        WHERE Email = :l.Email 
        LIMIT 1
    ];

    if (existingContacts.isEmpty()) {
        // Safe to convert - no duplicate found
        System.debug('Ready to convert: ' + l.FirstName + ' ' + l.LastName);
    } else {
        // Duplicate found - merge or update
        System.debug('Duplicate contact exists');
    }
}

Best Practices:

✅ Use Leads for all new prospects until they're qualified

✅ Implement lead scoring to prioritize follow-up

✅ Define clear qualification criteria (BANT: Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline)

✅ Use duplicate rules to prevent redundant Lead and Contact creation

✅ Train sales team on when to convert Leads vs create Contacts directly

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ All editions support Leads and Contacts
  • ✅ Professional and above: Lead assignment rules and web-to-lead

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How do Lead Assignment Rules work in Sales Cloud?
docs.text:
A: Lead Assignment Rules automatically route incoming leads to the right sales representatives based on predefined criteria, ensuring prompt follow-up and balanced workload distribution.

Key Components:

  • Assignment Rule: Container that holds multiple rule entries
  • Rule Entry: Specific criteria and assignment logic
  • Queue: Group of users who can work on assigned records
  • User Assignment: Direct assignment to specific user
  • Active Rule: Only one lead assignment rule can be active at a time

How It Works:

  • Leads are evaluated against rule entries in order
  • First matching criteria triggers assignment
  • If no criteria match, lead goes to default assignee or queue
  • Can be triggered via Web-to-Lead, API, or manual lead creation

Rule Entry Example:

Rule Entry 1: Enterprise Leads
Criteria: Annual Revenue >= 1,000,000 AND Employee Count >= 500
Assign To: Enterprise Sales Team Queue

Rule Entry 2: West Region Leads
Criteria: State = CA, OR, WA, NV, AZ
Assign To: West Region Sales Rep (User: John Smith)

Rule Entry 3: East Region Leads
Criteria: State = NY, NJ, CT, MA, PA
Assign To: East Region Sales Rep (User: Sarah Johnson)

Default Assignment: Inside Sales Queue

Implementation Example:

// Assign lead using assignment rules via Apex
Lead newLead = new Lead(
    FirstName = 'John',
    LastName = 'Doe',
    Company = 'Acme Corporation',
    Email = 'john.doe@acme.com',
    State = 'CA',
    AnnualRevenue = 5000000
);

// Use assignment rule
Database.DMLOptions dmo = new Database.DMLOptions();
dmo.AssignmentRuleHeader.useDefaultRule = true;
newLead.setOptions(dmo);

insert newLead;

// Lead will be assigned based on active assignment rule

Advanced Configuration:

  • Round Robin Assignment: Distribute leads evenly across team members
  • Territory-Based Assignment: Route based on geographic territories
  • Product-Based Assignment: Assign by product interest or expertise
  • Load Balancing: Consider current workload in assignment logic
  • After-Hours Assignment: Route to global teams based on time zones

Best Practices:

✅ Define clear routing criteria based on business requirements

✅ Use queues for team-based assignment and workload sharing

✅ Test assignment rules thoroughly before activation

✅ Monitor assignment patterns and adjust rules quarterly

✅ Document assignment logic for sales operations team

✅ Implement exception handling for leads that don't match any criteria

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Assignment rules are not enforced in batch Apex or data loader operations by default

⚠️ Must explicitly call assignment rules in Apex using Database.DMLOptions

Troubleshooting:

  • Leads not assigning: Check if assignment rule is active
  • Wrong assignment: Review rule order (first match wins)
  • API submissions: Ensure assignment rule header is included

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What are the stages of the Opportunity Sales Process?
docs.text:
A: The Opportunity Sales Process defines the stages a deal progresses through from initial qualification to close. Understanding and properly configuring these stages is critical for accurate pipeline management and forecasting.

Standard Opportunity Stages:

  • Prospecting: Initial research and outreach to potential customers
  • Qualification: Assessing if prospect is a good fit (BANT criteria)
  • Needs Analysis: Understanding customer requirements and pain points
  • Value Proposition: Presenting solution that addresses customer needs
  • Proposal/Price Quote: Delivering formal proposal with pricing
  • Negotiation/Review: Finalizing terms, pricing, and contract details
  • Closed Won: Deal successfully closed and contract signed
  • Closed Lost: Deal lost to competitor or no decision

Probability by Stage:

  • Prospecting: 10% probability of close
  • Qualification: 20% probability
  • Needs Analysis: 40% probability
  • Value Proposition: 60% probability
  • Proposal/Price Quote: 75% probability
  • Negotiation/Review: 90% probability
  • Closed Won: 100% (counted in closed revenue)
  • Closed Lost: 0% (removed from pipeline)

Example - Opportunity Management:

// Query opportunities in active pipeline
List<Opportunity> activeDeals = [
    SELECT Id, Name, AccountId, Account.Name, Amount, 
           StageName, CloseDate, Probability,
           (SELECT PricebookEntry.Product2.Name, Quantity, TotalPrice 
            FROM OpportunityLineItems)
    FROM Opportunity
    WHERE IsClosed = false
    AND StageName != 'Closed Lost'
    AND CloseDate >= TODAY
    AND CloseDate <= NEXT_90_DAYS
    ORDER BY CloseDate ASC, Amount DESC
];

// Calculate pipeline metrics
Decimal totalPipelineValue = 0;
Decimal weightedPipelineValue = 0;

for (Opportunity opp : activeDeals) {
    totalPipelineValue += opp.Amount;
    weightedPipelineValue += (opp.Amount * opp.Probability / 100);
}

System.debug('Total Pipeline: $' + totalPipelineValue);
System.debug('Weighted Pipeline: $' + weightedPipelineValue);

Path Configuration:

Salesforce Path provides visual guidance through sales stages:

  • Key Fields: Display important fields for each stage
  • Guidance: Stage-specific tips and best practices
  • Progress Indicator: Visual representation of deal progression
  • Required Fields: Enforce data collection at each stage

Stage Entry Criteria:

Qualification Stage Requirements:
✅ Budget confirmed
✅ Decision maker identified
✅ Pain points documented
✅ Timeline established

Proposal Stage Requirements:
✅ Formal presentation completed
✅ Technical requirements gathered
✅ Pricing approved by management
✅ Quote generated in Salesforce

Closed Won Requirements:
✅ Contract signed
✅ Purchase order received
✅ Start date confirmed
✅ Handoff to implementation team

Best Practices:

✅ Define clear exit criteria for each stage

✅ Align stages with actual sales methodology

✅ Use validation rules to enforce stage progression logic

✅ Configure Path to guide sales reps through stages

✅ Review stage probabilities quarterly based on historical win rates

✅ Implement stage-specific fields and layouts

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 1,000 opportunity stage values per org

⚠️ Close Date cannot be in the past for open opportunities (configurable)

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ All editions support opportunity management
  • ✅ Professional and above: Customizable sales processes
  • ✅ Enterprise and above: Multiple sales processes

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What are Opportunity Products and how do they work with Price Books?
docs.text:
A: Opportunity Products (OpportunityLineItems) represent the specific products or services being sold in a deal, while Price Books manage product pricing across different markets, segments, or scenarios.

Key Concepts:

  • Product2: The master product record (what you sell)
  • Price Book: Collection of products with associated prices
  • Price Book Entry: Specific product in a price book with defined price
  • Opportunity Line Item: Product added to an opportunity with quantity

Standard vs Custom Price Books:

  • Standard Price Book: Default price book containing list prices
  • Custom Price Books: Segment-specific pricing (Enterprise, Government, Partner, etc.)

Price Book Hierarchy:

Product: Salesforce Sales Cloud License
├── Standard Price Book Entry: $150/user/month
├── Enterprise Price Book Entry: $135/user/month (10% discount)
├── Government Price Book Entry: $120/user/month (20% discount)
└── Partner Price Book Entry: $105/user/month (30% discount)

Implementation Example:

// Step 1: Create or query product
Product2 product = new Product2(
    Name = 'Annual Support Package',
    ProductCode = 'SUP-ANNUAL-001',
    IsActive = true,
    Family = 'Support Services'
);
insert product;

// Step 2: Add product to Standard Price Book
Id standardPriceBookId = Test.isRunningTest() ? 
    Test.getStandardPricebookId() : 
    [SELECT Id FROM Pricebook2 WHERE IsStandard = true LIMIT 1].Id;

PricebookEntry standardPBE = new PricebookEntry(
    Product2Id = product.Id,
    Pricebook2Id = standardPriceBookId,
    UnitPrice = 10000,
    IsActive = true
);
insert standardPBE;

// Step 3: Add product to Custom Price Book
Pricebook2 customPriceBook = new Pricebook2(
    Name = 'Enterprise Price Book',
    IsActive = true
);
insert customPriceBook;

PricebookEntry customPBE = new PricebookEntry(
    Product2Id = product.Id,
    Pricebook2Id = customPriceBook.Id,
    UnitPrice = 8500, // 15% discount
    IsActive = true
);
insert customPBE;

// Step 4: Create opportunity with price book
Opportunity opp = new Opportunity(
    Name = 'Acme Corp - Annual Support',
    AccountId = accountId,
    StageName = 'Proposal/Price Quote',
    CloseDate = Date.today().addDays(30),
    Pricebook2Id = customPriceBook.Id
);
insert opp;

// Step 5: Add products to opportunity
OpportunityLineItem oli = new OpportunityLineItem(
    OpportunityId = opp.Id,
    PricebookEntryId = customPBE.Id,
    Quantity = 100,
    UnitPrice = 8500,
    Description = 'Annual support for 100 users'
);
insert oli;

// Calculate total: 100 users × $8,500 = $850,000

Product Schedules:

  • Quantity Schedules: Split quantity delivery across multiple dates
  • Revenue Schedules: Recognize revenue over time for subscriptions
  • Use Case: Annual contracts with monthly or quarterly billing

Best Practices:

✅ Always add products to Standard Price Book first

✅ Use custom price books for different customer segments

✅ Implement discounting policies with approval processes

✅ Use Product Families to organize product catalog

✅ Set up Revenue Schedules for subscription products

✅ Train sales team on price book selection criteria

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 2,000 OpportunityLineItems per Opportunity

⚠️ Must add product to Standard Price Book before adding to custom price books

Common Use Cases:

  • Software licensing with tiered pricing
  • Professional services with hourly rates
  • Hardware sales with volume discounts
  • Subscription products with revenue recognition

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: How does Collaborative Forecasting work in Sales Cloud?
docs.text:
A: Collaborative Forecasting enables sales teams to predict revenue, manage quotas, and track performance against targets through a structured forecasting process with management oversight and adjustments.

Forecasting Types:

  • Opportunity-based: Forecast based on individual opportunities in pipeline
  • Quota-based: Track progress toward assigned quotas
  • Territory-based: Aggregate forecasts across sales territories
  • Product Family: Forecast by product categories

Forecast Categories:

  • Pipeline: All open opportunities (not committed yet)
  • Best Case: Opportunities you're likely to close plus pipeline
  • Commit: Opportunities you're confident will close
  • Closed: Deals already won this period
  • Omitted: Opportunities excluded from forecast

Forecasting Hierarchy:

VP of Sales ($10M Quota)
├── Sales Manager West ($4M Quota)
│   ├── Sales Rep 1 ($1M Quota) - $800K Commit
│   ├── Sales Rep 2 ($1M Quota) - $950K Commit
│   ├── Sales Rep 3 ($1M Quota) - $750K Commit
│   └── Sales Rep 4 ($1M Quota) - $1.1M Commit
├── Sales Manager East ($3M Quota)
│   ├── Sales Rep 5 ($1M Quota) - $900K Commit
│   ├── Sales Rep 6 ($1M Quota) - $1.2M Commit
│   └── Sales Rep 7 ($1M Quota) - $850K Commit
└── Sales Manager Central ($3M Quota)
    ├── Sales Rep 8 ($1M Quota) - $950K Commit
    ├── Sales Rep 9 ($1M Quota) - $800K Commit
    └── Sales Rep 10 ($1M Quota) - $1.1M Commit

Manager Overrides:

  • Managers can adjust forecasts from direct reports
  • Override reasons tracked for accountability
  • Roll-up forecasts aggregate team submissions
  • Historical accuracy tracked per forecaster

Implementation Example:

// Query forecast data for current quarter
List<Opportunity> forecastOpps = [
    SELECT Id, Name, Amount, CloseDate, StageName,
           Probability, ForecastCategoryName, OwnerId, Owner.Name
    FROM Opportunity
    WHERE CloseDate = THIS_QUARTER
    AND IsClosed = false
    ORDER BY Amount DESC
];

// Group by forecast category
Map<String, Decimal> forecastByCategory = new Map<String, Decimal>{
    'Pipeline' => 0,
    'BestCase' => 0,
    'Commit' => 0,
    'Closed' => 0
};

for (Opportunity opp : forecastOpps) {
    String category = opp.ForecastCategoryName;
    if (forecastByCategory.containsKey(category)) {
        forecastByCategory.put(
            category, 
            forecastByCategory.get(category) + opp.Amount
        );
    }
}

System.debug('Pipeline: $' + forecastByCategory.get('Pipeline'));
System.debug('Best Case: $' + forecastByCategory.get('BestCase'));
System.debug('Commit: $' + forecastByCategory.get('Commit'));

Forecasting Process:

  • Week 1: Sales reps review opportunities and set forecast categories
  • Week 2: Managers review team forecasts and make adjustments
  • Week 3: Senior leadership reviews consolidated forecasts
  • Week 4: Final forecast submitted and tracked against actuals

Best Practices:

✅ Define clear criteria for each forecast category

✅ Conduct weekly forecast review meetings

✅ Track forecast accuracy metrics by rep and manager

✅ Align forecast periods with fiscal calendar

✅ Train team on consistent forecast categorization

✅ Use historical win rates to inform probability

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Forecasting available in: Professional, Enterprise, Unlimited, Developer
  • ✅ Customizable Forecasting: Enterprise and above
  • ✅ Territory-based Forecasting: Enterprise and above

Key Metrics:

  • Forecast Accuracy: (Actual Revenue / Forecasted Revenue) × 100
  • Win Rate: (Closed Won / Total Opportunities) × 100
  • Average Deal Size: Total Revenue / Number of Deals
  • Sales Cycle Length: Average days from creation to close

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What is Salesforce Service Cloud and what are its core capabilities?
docs.text:
A: Service Cloud is Salesforce's customer service and support platform designed to help organizations deliver exceptional customer experiences across multiple channels while improving agent productivity and customer satisfaction.

Core Capabilities:

  • Case Management: Track and resolve customer issues efficiently
  • Omni-Channel Routing: Intelligently route work to available agents
  • Service Console: Unified agent interface for productivity
  • Knowledge Base: Self-service articles and knowledge management
  • Live Chat & Messaging: Real-time customer communication
  • Field Service: Manage field technicians and on-site service
  • Self-Service Community: Customer portal for support
  • AI-Powered Service: Einstein for case classification and recommendations

Key Objects in Service Cloud:

  • Case: Customer service request or issue
  • Contact: Customer or end user
  • Account: Company or individual receiving service
  • Knowledge Article: Self-service content and documentation
  • Entitlement: Service level agreement and support coverage
  • Service Contract: Agreement defining service terms
  • Milestones: SLA tracking for response and resolution times

Service Cloud vs Sales Cloud:

  • Focus: Customer support and service vs sales and revenue
  • Metrics: CSAT, NPS, FCR, AHT vs quota attainment, win rate
  • Primary Object: Case vs Opportunity
  • User Types: Service agents vs sales representatives

Example Use Cases:

  • Customer support centers handling inquiries and complaints
  • Technical support teams resolving product issues
  • Field service organizations managing on-site repairs
  • Self-service portals for customer issue resolution
  • Warranty and RMA management

Salesforce Edition Requirements:

  • ✅ Service Cloud Essentials: Basic support for small teams (up to 10 users)
  • ✅ Professional: Core service features with case management
  • ✅ Enterprise: Advanced features with Omni-Channel and CTI
  • ✅ Unlimited: Premier support with all features

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Q: What are the different Service Cloud licenses and what features do they include?
docs.text:
A: Service Cloud offers various license types optimized for different user roles and functions in the customer service organization.

License Types:

  • Service Cloud User: Full-featured license for service agents
  • Service Cloud - One App: Includes Lightning Service Console only
  • Customer Community: License for external customer self-service
  • Customer Community Plus: Enhanced community features
  • Partner Community: License for partner support users
  • Field Service License: For mobile field technicians

Service Cloud User Features:

  • Case Management: Create, update, and close cases
  • Omni-Channel: Receive routed work items
  • Service Console: Access Lightning Service Console
  • Knowledge: Access and create knowledge articles
  • Live Agent: Handle chat sessions
  • CTI Integration: Computer telephony integration
  • Macros: Automate repetitive tasks
  • Email-to-Case: Convert emails to cases

Service Cloud - One App Features:

  • Access to Lightning Service Console only
  • Case management functionality
  • Knowledge article access
  • Limited customization options
  • Lower cost per user

Customer Community Features:

  • Self-service case creation and tracking
  • Knowledge base article search
  • Community discussions and collaboration
  • Mobile access to support portal
  • Limited API calls

Cost Considerations:

Typical Pricing Model (varies by contract):
- Service Cloud User: $150/user/month
- Service Cloud - One App: $75/user/month
- Customer Community: $10-15/user/month
- Field Service: Additional $50/user/month
- Einstein AI: Additional $50/user/month

License Allocation Strategy:

Customer Support Team (100 people):
├── Tier 1 Agents (60 agents): Service Cloud User
├── Tier 2 Specialists (30 agents): Service Cloud User
├── Supervisors (8 supervisors): Service Cloud User
├── Knowledge Authors (2 authors): Service Cloud User
├── Customers (10,000): Customer Community
└── Partners (200): Partner Community

Best Practices:

✅ Assess user needs before assigning license types

✅ Use Customer Community for scalable self-service

✅ Consider Service Cloud - One App for basic agent needs

✅ Monitor license usage to optimize costs

✅ Review and adjust license allocation quarterly

Governor Limits by License:

⚠️ Customer Community: 20 API calls per user per 24 hours

⚠️ Customer Community Plus: 200 API calls per user per 24 hours

⚠️ Service Cloud User: Standard API limits apply

docs.title: Q: How does Case Assignment and Routing work in Service Cloud?
docs.text:
A: Case Assignment and Routing ensures customer issues reach the right agent quickly based on skills, availability, channel, and business rules. Proper configuration improves first-contact resolution and customer satisfaction.

Assignment Methods:

  • Assignment Rules: Criteria-based automatic case routing
  • Omni-Channel: Skill-based and capacity-based routing
  • Queues: Group-based manual or automatic assignment
  • Round Robin: Distribute cases evenly across agents
  • Territory-Based: Route by geographic location or account territory

Case Assignment Rules:

Similar to Lead Assignment, but configured for Cases:

Rule Entry 1: VIP Customers
Criteria: Account.Type = 'Enterprise' AND Priority = 'High'
Assign To: VIP Support Queue

Rule Entry 2: Technical Issues
Criteria: Type = 'Technical' AND Product_Category__c = 'Software'
Assign To: Technical Support Team

Rule Entry 3: Billing Questions
Criteria: Type = 'Billing' OR Subject CONTAINS 'invoice'
Assign To: Billing Department Queue

Default Assignment: General Support Queue

Omni-Channel Routing:

Intelligent work distribution based on agent skills and capacity:

  • Skills-Based Routing: Match case requirements to agent skills
  • Capacity-Based Routing: Consider agent workload before assignment
  • Priority Routing: High-priority cases routed first
  • Presence-Based: Only route to available agents

Implementation Example:

// Create case with assignment rule
Case newCase = new Case(
    Subject = 'Unable to log into application',
    Description = 'Customer cannot access their account',
    Priority = 'High',
    Status = 'New',
    Origin = 'Web',
    Type = 'Technical',
    AccountId = accountId,
    ContactId = contactId
);

// Apply assignment rule during insert
Database.DMLOptions dmo = new Database.DMLOptions();
dmo.AssignmentRuleHeader.useDefaultRule = true;
newCase.setOptions(dmo);

insert newCase;

// Case will be automatically assigned based on active assignment rule

Escalation Rules:

Automatically escalate cases that aren't resolved within SLA:

Escalation Rule: Critical Cases
Criteria: Priority = 'Critical' AND Status != 'Closed'
├── Escalation Action 1 (2 hours): Email notification to supervisor
├── Escalation Action 2 (4 hours): Reassign to senior agent queue
└── Escalation Action 3 (8 hours): Create task for service manager

Queue Management:

// Query cases in queue
List<Case> queuedCases = [
    SELECT Id, CaseNumber, Subject, Priority, Status,
           CreatedDate, Account.Name, Contact.Name
    FROM Case
    WHERE OwnerId IN (
        SELECT Id FROM Group WHERE Type = 'Queue' AND Name = 'Technical Support'
    )
    AND Status != 'Closed'
    ORDER BY Priority DESC, CreatedDate ASC
];

// Accept case from queue (manual assignment)
Case caseToAccept = queuedCases[0];
caseToAccept.OwnerId = UserInfo.getUserId();
update caseToAccept;

Omni-Channel Configuration:

Service Channel: Case
├── Routing Priority: 1 (highest)
├── Capacity Weight: 1 case = 1 unit
├── Push Timeout: 30 seconds
└── Fallback Logic: Return to queue if not accepted

Skills Required:
├── Technical Support (Required)
├── Product Knowledge: CRM Software (Nice to have)
└── Language: Spanish (Optional)

Agent Configuration:
├── Service Presence Status: Available
├── Capacity: 5 units maximum
├── Current Workload: 3 cases (3 units used)
└── Available Capacity: 2 units

Best Practices:

✅ Define clear routing criteria based on case attributes

✅ Use Omni-Channel for real-time, intelligent routing

✅ Implement skill-based routing for specialized support

✅ Monitor queue wait times and adjust routing rules

✅ Balance workload across team members

✅ Set up escalation rules for SLA compliance

Governor Limits:

⚠️ Maximum 2,000 assignment rule entries across all active rules

⚠️ Assignment rules not enforced in Apex triggers unless explicitly called

Troubleshooting:

  • Cases not routing: Check if assignment rule is active
  • Wrong queue: Review rule criteria and order
  • Omni-Channel not working: Verify agent is available with capacity
